If your tract has activity in more than one formation, whatever historical statements you have for each help us build a complete picture, though we can reconstruct most of this directly from operator and county records if needed.

sections.title: Overlapping Woodford and Meramec development
sections.html: Much of the SCOOP and STACK fairway has stacked pay across the Woodford shale and the Meramec formation above it, sometimes developed by different operators targeting different benches under the same surface acreage, similar in principle to the Permian's stacked-bench structure but with its own distinct formation names and unit history. We check formation-by-formation activity for your specific section, since a tract can be actively producing from the Meramec while the deeper Woodford remains undeveloped, or vice versa, and that materially affects what's being valued.

sections.title: Title and closing in the core Oklahoma counties
sections.html: Core SCOOP and STACK counties, including Canadian, Kingfisher, Grady, and Garvin, generally maintain solid, reasonably digitized clerk records given how much recent transaction volume has passed through this area. Escrow holds funds until title is confirmed clean, and for producing tracts, we prorate the most recent royalty check to the closing date, consistent with standard practice across Oklahoma horizontal plays.

faqs.q: Is your tract in SCOOP, STACK, or both?
faqs.a: These plays overlap in parts of central Oklahoma, and some tracts sit within both fairways depending on formation. We confirm which play and formation applies to your specific section using current operator and permitting data before structuring an offer.

faqs.q: You were never approached to sign a lease. Can you still sell your minerals?
faqs.a: Likely yes, if you were force-pooled by an OCC order, which is common in these densely developed plays. We pull the pooling order to confirm your election and current status, then purchase the underlying interest with that order referenced in the closing documents.

faqs.q: Can the Meramec and Woodford under your tract be owned or valued differently?
faqs.a: They can be developed by different operators on different timelines even under the same acreage. We check activity separately for each formation rather than assuming uniform development across your full stacked interest.

faqs.q: How fast do SCOOP and STACK closings typically move?
faqs.a: Core counties here generally have solid, digitized records given the volume of recent transactions, so closing timelines tend to be on the faster end once title and, if applicable, pooling order status are confirmed.

faqs.q: Do you buy interests that are only leased, not yet producing?
faqs.a: Yes, we evaluate leased, permitted acreage in these plays regularly, pricing against documented permitting and operator activity for your specific section.

faqs.q: Does the SCOOP and STACK naming convention affect what you actually own?
faqs.a: No, these are industry play names describing geographic and geologic trends, not legal ownership categories. What matters for your sale is the specific formation and unit tied to your tract.

faqs.q: Are Grady and Garvin Counties developed the same way as Canadian and Kingfisher?
faqs.a: Formation depth and target intervals shift somewhat across the fairway, so activity isn't identical county to county. We confirm current operator and formation activity for your specific section.

items.name: Permian Basin Mineral Rights
items.meta: Selling Permian Basin minerals in the Midland or Delaware sub-basin? Learn how stacked-pay diligence, unit allocation, and closing actually work.

sections.html:
The Permian Basin is really two basins stitched together under one name, and the first question in any purchase is which side of it your minerals sit on.

When someone says they own "Permian Basin" minerals, that tells a buyer almost nothing about value or process until we know whether the tract sits in the Midland Basin or the Delaware Basin, and which county line it falls on. The two sub-basins have different operators, different stacked formations, and different title histories, so the purchase workflow bends around geography from the first phone call.

What stays constant is the transaction shape: we pull the deed and lease chain, confirm what interest you actually hold, run it against current production or permitting activity, and structure a purchase and sale agreement with a closing date tied to how clean the title comes back.

sections.title: Why stacked pay changes the diligence checklist
sections.html:
Permian tracts commonly have three, four, or more separate producing intervals stacked under the same surface acreage — Spraberry, Wolfcamp A through D, Bone Spring, Avalon, and older conventional zones below all of it. A single county road and 40-acre tract might have one horizontal well draining the upper Wolfcamp and a completely different operator running a unit through the Bone Spring two thousand feet deeper. That means diligence isn't a single lookup; it's a bench-by-bench review of every formation with an active or permitted unit touching your acreage.

This is also where valuation gets misread by sellers who compare notes with a neighbor. Two adjoining tracts can carry very different worth if one sits under three completed benches and the other only has permits filed on one. We walk through the permitting and completion history bench by bench during diligence, not because it's academic, but because it directly changes what interest is actually being priced.

sections.title: Allocation wells and how they affect your check
sections.html:
Much of the recent Permian horizontal development uses allocation wells, where a single wellbore crosses multiple leases and production is allocated back to each tract by a formula tied to lateral footage rather than a formal pooling order. If your minerals are under an allocation well, the division order analyst needs the allocation schedule, not only the unit designation, to confirm your decimal interest is correct before we close.

We request the allocation well agreement and the operator's decimal calculation as part of diligence on any Midland or Delaware Basin tract that's already producing. Mismatches between the recorded allocation and what a royalty statement is actually paying are common enough that we check this before making an offer, not after.

sections.title: Closing mechanics on producing versus non-producing tracts
sections.html:
On a producing Permian tract, escrow holds funds until the title runs clean and the operator confirms in writing that a transfer order can be processed, and we typically prorate the most recent royalty check based on the closing date so neither side collects for a period they didn't own the interest. On acreage that's leased but not yet producing — common on the Delaware side where permitting has outpaced completion — closing is simpler because there's no revenue stream to prorate, but we still confirm the lease hasn't expired and that no held-by-production clause is in dispute.

County clerk turnaround varies a lot across the Permian footprint. Midland and Ector County records are largely digitized; some of the smaller New Mexico counties on the Delaware side still require a courthouse visit to pull the full chain, which we build into the closing timeline up front so nobody is surprised by a two-week gap.

sections.title: What we ask for before pricing your interest
sections.html: A current division order and recent royalty statements are the most useful documents for a producing Permian interest, since they let us confirm your decimal interest against the active spacing or allocation unit quickly. For non-producing, permitted acreage, we work primarily from the lease and current permit filings for your specific section.

faqs.q: How do you know if you're in the Midland Basin or the Delaware Basin?
faqs.a: It comes down to county and, sometimes, which side of the Central Basin Platform your section falls on. We confirm this from your deed's legal description during the first review; it's one of the first things we check because it determines which formations and operators are even relevant.

faqs.q: Does owning under multiple stacked benches mean a faster closing?
faqs.a: Not necessarily faster, but it usually means more diligence line items since each bench can have its own operator, lease, and production history. We still hold to a normal escrow timeline; there's just more to verify before funds release.

faqs.q: What if your minerals are permitted but no well has been drilled yet?
faqs.a: We still purchase permitted, non-producing Permian interests. Valuation depends heavily on how advanced the permit is and which operator holds it, so pricing conversations are framed around activity and comparable recent transactions rather than a fixed number.

faqs.q: Who handles the division order after closing?
faqs.a: Once title transfers, we submit the recorded deed and required documentation directly to the operator's division order department. You aren't responsible for that paperwork; we track it through to confirmation that future checks are issued correctly.

faqs.q: Can two adjoining tracts really be priced very differently?
faqs.a: Yes, if one sits under more active or completed benches than the other. We price against documented formation-level activity for your specific tract, not neighborhood comparisons.

items.name: Midland Basin Mineral Rights
items.meta: How a Midland Basin mineral purchase moves from title check to closing, including horizontal DSU allocation, Spraberry and Wolfcamp bench review.

sections.html:
On the Midland side of the Permian, most of what you own is defined by a drilling and spacing unit, not the four corners printed on your original deed.

The Midland Basin is the shallower, eastern half of the Permian, and it's been under horizontal development longer than almost anywhere else in the country, which means most tracts here already have a production history to review rather than a blank permit file. That history is actually helpful for a buyer — it gives us royalty statements, division order decimals, and completion dates to work from instead of estimating from scratch.

The purchase itself follows the same core steps as any mineral sale — title review, offer, purchase and sale agreement, escrow, recording — but the diligence work leans hard on reconciling your deeded acreage against the horizontal drilling and spacing units that actually control your interest today.

sections.title: Reading a Midland Basin division order correctly
sections.html:
Because Midland Basin wells are almost always horizontal and often drilled in multi-well pads, your decimal interest is calculated against the spacing unit acreage, not your raw net mineral acres. A seller who owns 40 net mineral acres in a 640-acre unit is being paid on a fraction of that unit, and the division order should reflect exactly that math. Before we make an offer on a producing tract, we pull the division order and confirm the unit size, your net acres, and any royalty burden stacking from prior conveyances all line up.

Where this gets complicated is legacy tracts that have been sold or split among heirs multiple times since the original 1940s or 1950s lease. Each conveyance in the chain can carry a different fractional reservation, and an error two owners back can still be affecting your check today. We trace that chain during diligence rather than taking the current royalty statement at face value.

sections.title: Spraberry and Wolfcamp bench activity
sections.html:
Midland Basin acreage is typically developed across the Spraberry and multiple Wolfcamp benches, and operators here have been drilling long enough that most core Midland, Martin, and Howard County tracts have at least one completed well with a real production curve to evaluate, rather than a speculative permit. That's useful for pricing conversations because we can look at actual monthly volumes and decline behavior instead of projecting from a type curve alone.

Flank areas toward the basin edges still see permitting activity without full development, so the same tract-by-tract, bench-by-bench check applies — we're not assuming activity based on the county name, we're confirming it against the current permit and completion record for your specific section.

sections.title: Escrow and proration on producing interests
sections.html: Because most Midland Basin tracts we buy are already receiving royalty checks, closing includes a proration step: the most recent check gets split based on the exact closing date, so you keep everything earned before the sale and we begin collecting after. Funds sit in escrow until the deed is confirmed recordable and title comes back clean, which for Midland, Martin, and Reagan Counties usually means digitized courthouse records and a shorter turnaround than more rural counties elsewhere in the basin.

sections.title: What we ask for before pricing your interest
sections.html:
A current division order and the two or three most recent royalty statements are typically enough for us to confirm your decimal interest and current production level with confidence, since Midland Basin operators generally maintain well-organized, digitized records. If your interest passed through several conveyances since the original mid-20th-century lease, any prior title opinion or attorney correspondence you have is helpful, though not required.

We can trace the full chain independently through county records if your own file is incomplete, which is common for interests that have changed hands multiple times over the decades.

faqs.q: Your deed lists 20 acres, but you're only paid on a fraction of that. Why?
faqs.a: Your royalty is calculated against your share of the spacing unit, not your raw acreage. If your 20 net mineral acres sit inside a 640-acre unit, your decimal reflects that ratio times your royalty fraction, which is normal and something we verify against the division order before buying.

faqs.q: Does the Wolfcamp have multiple separately owned benches?
faqs.a: The Wolfcamp is often split into Wolfcamp A, B, C, and sometimes D benches, each potentially operated or permitted separately. We check which specific bench any active or planned well targets, since that determines what's actually generating revenue against your interest.

faqs.q: How current does your royalty statement need to be to sell?
faqs.a: We typically ask for the most recent two to three months of statements to gauge current activity, plus the division order. Older or missing statements aren't disqualifying; we can still work from the operator's current production record.

faqs.q: What slows a Midland Basin closing down the most?
faqs.a: Usually an incomplete heirship chain from a prior generation, not the operator or the county. Once title is confirmed clean, closing in this basin tends to move faster than average because most county records here are already digitized.

faqs.q: Can the closing desk work with an owner's operator to confirm the decimal interest?
faqs.a: Yes, we routinely verify decimal interests directly against operator division order records rather than relying solely on documents you provide.

items.name: Delaware Basin Mineral Rights
items.meta: Delaware Basin minerals in Texas or New Mexico: how deeper stacked-pay diligence, state trust land leases, and closing differ from Midland Basin sales.

sections.html:
The Delaware Basin runs deeper and thicker than its neighbor to the east, and if your minerals sit on the New Mexico side, state land ownership can be part of the picture before we ever get to yours.

The Delaware Basin is the western, deeper half of the Permian, stretching from West Texas into southeast New Mexico, and it carries more stacked pay per section than almost any other U.S. play — Bone Spring, Avalon, Wolfcamp, and Delaware sand intervals can all be separately targeted under the same acreage. For a buyer, that means diligence has more layers to check, and for a seller, it usually means more potential value if multiple benches are active.

The core purchase process doesn't change: title review, offer, agreement, escrow, closing. What changes is how much operator and formation-level checking happens before an offer is made, and, on the New Mexico side, whether adjacent state trust land leasing affects unit configuration around your tract.

sections.title: Why Delaware Basin diligence takes longer per bench
sections.html:
A single Delaware Basin section can have separate horizontal units targeting the Wolfcamp A, Wolfcamp B, second Bone Spring, and third Bone Spring — four distinct spacing units, four distinct operators potentially, four distinct division orders. Before we make an offer, we build a formation-by-formation activity map for your specific tract: which benches have permits, which have completed wells, and which are still undeveloped. That map is what actually drives the offer, not the county name alone.

This is also where sellers sometimes overvalue based on general basin reputation. Being "in the Delaware Basin" doesn't mean every bench under your acreage is active; some flank tracts have one productive interval and three that remain untested. We price against what's documented, and we're upfront about which benches show real activity versus speculative permitting.

sections.title: New Mexico state trust land and title complexity
sections.html:
On the New Mexico side of the basin, particularly Eddy and Lea Counties, checkerboard sections of state trust land administered by the New Mexico State Land Office sit interspersed with private and federal minerals. If a horizontal unit crosses state trust acreage, the operator's lease with the State Land Office follows separate royalty terms and reporting than a private lease, and it can affect how a unit gets configured around your tract. We confirm during diligence whether your minerals border or fall within a unit that includes state trust acreage, since it changes what division order documentation we need to pull.

Texas-side Delaware Basin counties like Reeves, Culberson, and Loving don't carry that state trust overlay, so title review there tracks closer to standard Permian process — deed chain, lease status, and current operator confirmation.

sections.title: Escrow, proration, and closing timelines
sections.html: As with any producing Permian tract, escrow holds funds until title is confirmed clean and recordable, and we prorate the most recent royalty check to the closing date. Delaware Basin counties on the Texas side are generally well digitized; several New Mexico counties still require direct courthouse research to complete a full chain of title, which we factor into the closing schedule from the start rather than discovering mid-transaction.

sections.title: What we ask for before pricing your tract
sections.html:
For a producing Delaware Basin interest, we request the current division order and recent royalty statements to confirm your decimal interest against the active unit or units. For non-producing, permitted acreage, we work primarily from the lease and any permit filings tied to your section, since there's no royalty statement yet to review.

Where a tract borders New Mexico state trust land, we also confirm the State Land Office lease terms for the relevant unit, since that documentation informs how we assess the unit's overall configuration and activity level around your minerals.

faqs.q: How many formations might be active under your Delaware Basin tract?
faqs.a: It varies, but two to four separately targeted benches under the same section isn't unusual. We check permit and completion records for each formation individually rather than assuming activity in one bench means activity everywhere.

faqs.q: Does bordering state trust land in New Mexico affect your minerals?
faqs.a: It can affect how a spacing unit is configured if your tract borders or overlaps state trust acreage, but it doesn't change your ownership. We confirm the unit boundaries and documentation during diligence so there's no confusion at closing.

faqs.q: Is Delaware Basin acreage worth more than Midland Basin acreage?
faqs.a: It depends entirely on documented activity for the specific tract, not the sub-basin name. Some Delaware acreage has more stacked, active benches; some Midland acreage has longer production history. We price against your specific formation-level activity, not basin reputation.

faqs.q: How long does a New Mexico county closing typically take?
faqs.a: Several Delaware Basin counties in New Mexico still require in-person courthouse research rather than digitized lookup, which can add one to two weeks to the title timeline. We build that into the schedule up front so it doesn't cause a surprise delay.

faqs.q: Do you buy non-producing, leased-only Delaware Basin acreage?
faqs.a: Yes, we regularly purchase leased but not yet producing interests. Pricing reflects the permit activity and operator involvement on your specific section rather than existing royalty income.

items.name: Barnett Shale Mineral Rights
items.meta: Selling Fort Worth-area Barnett Shale minerals? Learn how legacy 2000s leases, stripper-well decline, and urban surface issues shape the sale.

sections.html:
The Barnett Shale was the first major shale gas play in the country, and that means most leases here are now old enough to have grandchildren, which shows up directly in title work.

Centered around Fort Worth and the surrounding North Texas counties, the Barnett Shale kicked off the modern shale gas era in the early 2000s, and today most of the wells drilled during that first wave are well into decline, with many now producing at stripper-well levels. For a mineral owner, that means a Barnett Shale interest today usually looks different than it did fifteen years ago — a smaller, steadier check reflecting mature gas production rather than an active development phase.

That maturity actually simplifies some things and complicates others: production history is long and well documented, but title chains have often passed through multiple heirs since the original lease was signed, and some of the field's development happened inside city limits, which brings its own surface-access history into the picture.

sections.title: Legacy leases and multi-generation title chains
sections.html:
Barnett Shale leases signed in the mid-2000s have frequently outlived the original owner, passing through inheritance one or more times since. Because Tarrant, Denton, Johnson, and surrounding county records have been reasonably well maintained and digitized for some time, tracing that chain is usually manageable, but we still confirm every conveyance and any probate or affidavit of heirship that moved the interest along the way before structuring an offer.

Where this gets slower is when an original owner passed without a will and the interest was never formally probated, leaving several living heirs each holding an undivided fractional share without clean documentation. We can still work with this, but it typically means gathering signatures or documentation from multiple family members before a sale can close.

sections.title: What stripper-well decline means for your check
sections.html: Many Barnett Shale wells have declined to what's classified as stripper-well production, meaning low but often still economically viable volumes that can continue for years. This shows up as a modest, relatively stable royalty check rather than the larger, faster-declining payments typical of newer shale plays. We evaluate current production data against the well's decline history to assess how much continued life the interest likely has, which is central to how the tract is priced.

sections.title: Urban and suburban surface considerations
sections.html: A meaningful share of Barnett Shale development happened inside or near Fort Worth's city limits and surrounding suburbs, which brought city drilling ordinances and surface-use agreements into the picture in ways more rural basins don't typically see. Those ordinances don't change your mineral ownership, but they can affect whether an operator pursues any future development on already-drilled acreage, which we factor into our read of a tract's remaining upside beyond its current production.

sections.title: Documents that speed up a Barnett Shale review
sections.html:
A recent royalty check stub or statement is usually enough for us to identify the operator, well, and unit tied to your interest and start pulling production history. If your family has held the interest since the original 2000s lease, an original lease copy is helpful but not required, since we can retrieve it from the county clerk's record directly.

For interests that passed through inheritance without formal probate, we'll walk you through what documentation, such as an affidavit of heirship, is typically needed so the sale can close cleanly without requiring a full probate proceeding in most cases.

faqs.q: Is your Barnett Shale interest still worth selling if the well is old?
faqs.a: Yes. Mature, stripper-level production is still an income-generating interest, and we regularly purchase these. Pricing reflects the current production level and expected remaining life rather than the well's original output from years ago.

faqs.q: Your family never formally divided the mineral interest after your grandparent passed. Can we still sell?
faqs.a: Often yes, but it usually requires documentation such as an affidavit of heirship or probate records establishing each heir's share before closing. We can walk your family through what's needed rather than requiring you to sort it out first.

faqs.q: Do city drilling ordinances in Fort Worth affect your ownership?
faqs.a: No, they affect where and how an operator can drill, not who owns the minerals underneath. They can factor into how much future development is realistic on already-developed acreage, which we consider during valuation.

faqs.q: Why is your Barnett Shale check smaller than it was years ago?
faqs.a: Barnett Shale wells generally follow a steep early decline curve typical of shale gas, followed by a long, low-volume stripper-well tail. A smaller, steadier check today usually reflects normal decline behavior rather than an issue with your interest.

faqs.q: Do you need to complete probate before selling an inherited interest?
faqs.a: Not always. In many cases an affidavit of heirship or similar documentation is sufficient to establish your share, and we'll advise on what's actually needed for your specific situation.

faqs.q: Is there a minimum interest size you'll purchase in this basin?
faqs.a: We evaluate interests of varying sizes, including smaller fractional shares common after multiple generations of inheritance. Send us what you have and we'll confirm whether it's a fit.

items.name: Eagle Ford Shale Mineral Rights
items.meta: Selling South Texas Eagle Ford minerals? Learn how held-by-production status, oil/gas window position, and RRC unitization affect the sale.

sections.html:
Most Eagle Ford leases still active today were signed during the original 2010 to 2014 boom, so the first question in diligence is usually whether that old lease is still legally held.

The Eagle Ford Shale runs across a broad band of South Texas counties, and it's mature enough now that almost every tract we evaluate has an existing lease with real history behind it rather than a fresh permit. That maturity is actually the central fact of an Eagle Ford transaction: production has often declined from its early peak, and whether the original lease is still held by production is the first thing diligence needs to nail down.

The Eagle Ford is also unusual for how much it varies across its own footprint — from the oil window in the north through the volatile oil and condensate window in the middle to the dry gas window toward the Mexican border — and that position changes both what's being produced and what a reasonable offer looks like.

sections.title: Held by production and lease status review
sections.html:
A lease signed during the original Eagle Ford boom is typically held past its primary term as long as the well it's tied to keeps producing in paying quantities. If a well has gone to marginal, stripper-level production, or has been shut in for a stretch, that can raise a real question about whether the lease is still validly held, which affects whether the operator has ongoing rights to your minerals or whether they've reverted. We pull the current production record and lease terms together during diligence specifically to answer this before pricing an offer.

This is one of the more consequential checks in an Eagle Ford purchase because it directly changes what's being sold — a mineral interest under a solidly held, producing lease is a different asset than one where the lease may be lapsing, even on the same tract.

sections.title: What we ask for before pricing your interest
sections.html:
A recent royalty statement and the original lease are the most useful starting documents, since together they let us confirm both your decimal interest and whether the lease's held-by-production status is likely secure. If your well has gone to marginal or intermittent production, we'll also ask about any recent operator correspondence regarding the well's status.

Where an interest has passed through inheritance since the original 2010s lease, we help identify what documentation is needed to establish clean title before closing, which is a common step given how many years have now passed since much of the Eagle Ford's original leasing wave.

sections.title: Oil window position and what it means for royalty behavior
sections.html: Where your tract sits within the Eagle Ford's oil-to-gas gradient affects the character of your royalty check. Oil window counties tend to show steeper initial decline curves with strong early payments that taper faster; the gas window toward the southwest produces more gradually declining volumes tied to gas pricing rather than oil pricing. We review your specific production history against your window position rather than assuming Eagle Ford-wide behavior, since a check from a condensate-window well and one from a dry-gas-window well respond very differently to commodity price swings.

sections.title: Texas Railroad Commission unitization and title
sections.html: Eagle Ford units are governed by Railroad Commission of Texas unitization rules, and because this play has been drilled in phases over more than a decade, some tracts have gone through multiple unit reconfigurations as operators refined their spacing. We check the current RRC unit designation against your original lease and any amendments, since older leases sometimes predate a later unit boundary change that affects your allocated share.

faqs.q: How do you know if your Eagle Ford lease is still held by production?
faqs.a: We check the well's current production status against the lease's habendum clause terms. If the well is still producing in paying quantities, the lease is generally still held; if production has stopped or dropped to marginal levels for an extended period, that status needs closer review before we structure an offer.

faqs.q: Does your county tell you whether you're in the oil or gas window?
faqs.a: Largely, yes. Eagle Ford window position tracks fairly closely with county and even sub-county location, and we confirm your specific position against production data rather than county name alone, since the transition zones aren't perfectly aligned with county lines.

faqs.q: Why has your Eagle Ford royalty check declined so much since it started?
faqs.a: Shale wells in this play typically show a steep initial decline curve, especially in the oil window, so a large early payment followed by a much smaller ongoing check is normal well behavior, not necessarily a sign of a problem with your interest.

faqs.q: Can you buy minerals under an older, marginally producing Eagle Ford well?
faqs.a: Yes, we evaluate these regularly. The offer reflects the current, often lower production level and any lease status questions, but marginal production doesn't disqualify a tract from purchase.

faqs.q: What if your Eagle Ford lease is close to its primary term expiring?
faqs.a: We check current production status directly, since paying production generally extends a lease past its primary term. We'll explain exactly where your specific lease stands before making an offer.

items.name: Haynesville Shale Mineral Rights
items.meta: Selling Haynesville Shale gas minerals in East Texas or Louisiana? Learn how deep-well economics and post-production cost deductions affect a sale.

sections.html:
Haynesville wells are drilled deeper and under higher pressure than most U.S. gas plays, and the deduction line on your royalty statement deserves a closer look than most owners give it.

The Haynesville Shale sits under East Texas and northwest Louisiana, one of the most prolific dry gas plays in the country, with wells commonly drilled past 12,000 feet and completed at high pressure and cost. Because it's a gas play rather than an oil play, Haynesville royalty income moves with natural gas pricing specifically, which has swung more sharply over the past several years than oil, and that volatility is worth understanding before you evaluate an offer on your minerals.

The purchase process itself is standard — title, offer, escrow, closing — but two things get extra attention here: the post-production cost deductions showing up on gas royalty statements, and, on the Louisiana side, how the state's forced unitization process differs from Texas.

sections.title: Post-production cost deductions and how to read your statement
sections.html: Gas royalty statements commonly show deductions for gathering, compression, processing, and transportation costs incurred after the gas leaves the wellhead, and the specific language in your lease determines how much of that cost can legally be passed through to you as the royalty owner. Some older Haynesville leases have more favorable, less deduction-friendly language than newer ones, and the gap between gross wellhead value and your net check can be substantial depending on which lease terms actually apply to your interest. We review the lease's deduction language against the statement during diligence, since it directly affects what net income the interest is generating and, in turn, how we value it.

sections.title: Louisiana forced unitization versus Texas practice
sections.html: On the Louisiana side of the play, the state's Office of Conservation can establish a drilling unit and force unleased or nonconsenting owners into it, similar in effect to Oklahoma's pooling process but administered under Louisiana's own conservation statutes. If your minerals are in a Louisiana parish and you were unitized rather than leased directly, we pull the unitization order to confirm your status and payment terms before structuring a purchase. Texas-side Haynesville tracts in counties like Panola, Harrison, and San Augustine follow the Railroad Commission's more typical voluntary leasing and unit designation process.

sections.title: Deep-well economics and what that means for activity
sections.html: Because Haynesville wells cost significantly more to drill and complete than shallower plays, operator activity here tends to track gas pricing more sensitively than most basins — development accelerates when gas prices support the higher breakeven cost and slows when they don't. We check current permitting and rig activity for your specific parish or county as part of diligence rather than assuming a constant pace of development, since Haynesville activity has moved in more visible cycles than steadier oil-weighted basins.

sections.title: What we ask for before pricing your interest
sections.html:
A recent gas royalty statement showing both gross value and itemized deductions is the most useful document for us to review, since it lets us assess your actual net royalty position rather than just gross production volume. The original lease, particularly its royalty and post-production cost clauses, is equally important for confirming whether current deductions are consistent with what was agreed to.

For Louisiana-side interests brought into a unit by an Office of Conservation order rather than a lease, we request that order directly as part of confirming your current terms and payment status.

faqs.q: Why is the deduction line on your Haynesville royalty statement so large?
faqs.a: Gas requires more downstream processing and transportation than oil before it reaches a sellable point, and many leases allow the operator to pass a share of those post-production costs back to royalty owners. We check your specific lease language to confirm the deductions being applied are consistent with what was actually agreed to.

faqs.q: You were unitized in Louisiana without signing a lease. Can you still sell?
faqs.a: Yes. A Louisiana Office of Conservation unitization order establishes your terms similarly to a lease, and we can purchase the underlying interest. We pull the order during diligence to confirm your status and current payment terms.

faqs.q: Does gas price volatility affect your mineral value more than it would for oil minerals?
faqs.a: Haynesville income tracks natural gas pricing specifically, which has moved in wider swings than oil recently. We factor current and recent pricing trends into valuation rather than relying on a single point-in-time snapshot.

faqs.q: Is your Haynesville interest less valuable because the wells are so deep and expensive?
faqs.a: Deeper, higher-cost wells affect operator drilling economics, not your ownership. Valuation is based on documented production, lease terms, and current activity for your specific tract rather than well cost alone.

faqs.q: Can the closing desk review a lease for improper deductions?
faqs.a: Yes, reviewing your specific royalty clause and deduction language against your statement is a standard part of our diligence before we structure an offer.

faqs.q: Do you buy Haynesville interests where the operator has slowed drilling recently?
faqs.a: Yes. Slower current activity doesn't disqualify a tract, and we price against documented current production and lease status rather than requiring active new drilling on your specific unit.

items.name: Fayetteville Shale Mineral Rights
items.meta: Selling Arkansas Fayetteville Shale gas minerals? Honest guidance on today's slowed activity, legacy leases, and how a purchase still works.

sections.html:
Fayetteville Shale drilling has slowed substantially since its mid-2010s peak, and an honest conversation about that is the right starting point before we talk about your minerals.

The Fayetteville Shale in north-central Arkansas was one of the earlier major shale gas plays, developed heavily through the late 2000s and into the mid-2010s before natural gas pricing and the emergence of lower-cost plays elsewhere caused operator activity to slow considerably. Today, most Fayetteville tracts we evaluate are under legacy leases with long production histories, often on wells that have declined well past their early peak, and some units in the play have seen operators reduce activity or shift focus elsewhere entirely.

That's not a reason to avoid selling — mature, low-decline gas production is still a real income stream and still has value — but it does mean the conversation should be grounded in what's actually happening on your tract right now rather than the play's more active years.

sections.title: What current activity in the Fayetteville actually looks like
sections.html: Compared to its peak development years, permitting and new drilling activity across the Fayetteville Shale footprint have slowed considerably, and some wells drilled during the boom have been shut in or plugged as they reached the end of their economic life. We check the current operational status of the specific well or unit tied to your minerals — actively producing, shut in, or plugged and abandoned — since that status materially changes both the interest's current income and its realistic near-term outlook.

sections.title: Long-tail production and what it means for valuation
sections.html: Wells that have been producing for a decade or more in this play have typically settled into a long, low-decline tail of gas production rather than the steep early decline curve seen in a newer well. That can mean smaller checks than the play's early years but also a more predictable, stable production profile going forward, which we weigh directly in how we price a legacy Fayetteville interest — we're not comparing it to newer, higher-decline shale plays, we're evaluating it on its own mature production curve.

sections.title: Title review on older Arkansas leases
sections.html: Because most active Fayetteville leases were signed well over a decade ago, title chains here commonly include at least one generation of inheritance since the original owner signed. Arkansas county clerk records in the core Fayetteville counties like Van Buren, Cleburne, and Conway are generally accessible, and we confirm the full chain of title and any heirship documentation as part of standard diligence before making an offer.

sections.title: What we ask for before pricing your interest
sections.html:
A recent royalty statement is the most useful document for confirming current status, since it tells us immediately whether the well is producing, at what level, and under what operator. If you haven't received a statement recently, that itself is informative, and we'll check directly with the operator or Arkansas Oil and Gas Commission records to confirm whether the well is shut in or plugged.

We also review the original lease terms, since some legacy Fayetteville leases include provisions around shut-in royalties or continuous development that can affect how a currently idle well's status should be interpreted.

faqs.q: Is the Fayetteville Shale still an active play?
faqs.a: Development has slowed substantially from its mid-2010s peak, and some operators have reduced activity or moved on to other basins. Existing wells continue producing, often at mature, lower-decline volumes, and we evaluate your specific tract's current status directly rather than relying on the play's earlier reputation.

faqs.q: Your well seems to be producing much less than it used to. Is it still worth selling?
faqs.a: Yes, mature, low-decline gas production still generates real income and still has value. We price based on the well's current, documented production rather than its historical peak.

faqs.q: What if your well has been shut in or plugged?
faqs.a: We check current operational status as part of diligence. A shut-in well may still hold value depending on the reason and outlook; a plugged well changes the picture significantly, and we're upfront about how that affects an offer.

faqs.q: How old are typical active leases in this play?
faqs.a: Most active Fayetteville leases date to the play's main development period roughly a decade to fifteen years ago, so title chains commonly include at least one round of inheritance, which we account for in standard diligence.

faqs.q: Will the closing desk state plainly when a well appears near the end of its life?
faqs.a: Yes. We price based on documented current status and are direct about what a well's production trend suggests, rather than presenting an inflated picture.

faqs.q: Should you expect an offer close to what neighbors received years ago?
faqs.a: Not necessarily. Activity and pricing have changed substantially since this play's peak years, so we base an offer on your tract's current documented status rather than historical comparisons from a much more active period.

faqs.q: Are there still any active operators drilling new wells in this play?
faqs.a: Activity is much reduced from the play's peak, though some operators maintain limited activity in select areas. We check current permitting for your specific county rather than assuming basin-wide status.

items.name: Bakken Mineral Rights
items.meta: Selling North Dakota or Montana Bakken minerals? Learn how Three Forks bench stacking and Fort Berthold trust land affect a purchase.

sections.html:
If your Bakken minerals sit within the Fort Berthold Reservation, the sale may need Bureau of Indian Affairs sign-off in addition to the usual county paperwork.

The Bakken and underlying Three Forks formation across western North Dakota and eastern Montana represent one of the largest horizontal oil plays in the country, developed intensively since the mid-2000s with dense, multi-well pad drilling. Most Bakken tracts we evaluate today have substantial production history, since this basin moved from early delineation to full-scale development faster than almost any other modern shale play. Ownership here ranges from straightforward private fee minerals to interests tied to tribal trust and allotted land within the Fort Berthold Reservation, home to the Mandan, Hidatsa, and Arikara Nation, which changes the transfer process significantly.

The standard purchase sequence applies across the basin, but confirming ownership type and, separately, which formation bench your interest is tied to are the two things that shape everything else.

sections.title: Fort Berthold trust and allotted minerals
sections.html: A significant share of Bakken and Three Forks development sits on or near the Fort Berthold Reservation, where minerals can be held in tribal trust or as individual Indian allotments rather than private fee ownership. Transferring a trust or allotted interest requires approval through the Bureau of Indian Affairs, a process with its own documentation requirements and timeline distinct from a standard county deed transfer. We confirm ownership status at the start of diligence for any Fort Berthold-area tract, since this determines the entire path to closing.

sections.title: Middle Bakken and Three Forks bench stacking
sections.html: Much of the basin's core development targets both the Middle Bakken and the Three Forks formation immediately below it, and the Three Forks itself is often subdivided into multiple separately targeted benches in the most active areas. A single spacing unit may have wells completed in more than one of these intervals over time as operators refined their development plans, so we review the full well history for your specific unit, not only the most recent well, since older and newer wells can be tied to different formation benches with different division order treatment.

sections.title: Proration and closing on producing North Dakota tracts
sections.html: For producing tracts in core counties like McKenzie, Mountrail, and Williams, North Dakota county records are generally well organized, and closing follows the standard sequence of title confirmation, escrow, and proration of the most recent royalty check to the closing date. For interests touching Fort Berthold trust land, we build the additional BIA approval timeline into the schedule from the outset so expectations are set correctly before closing begins.

sections.title: Non-operated interests and working interest sellers
sections.html:
While most of what we purchase in the Bakken is royalty or mineral interest, some owners also hold small non-operated working interests from early participation elections, particularly on Fort Berthold-adjacent units where owners were offered a working interest option during pooling or leasing. Working interest carries drilling and operating cost exposure that royalty interest doesn't, so we evaluate it under a different framework, reviewing lease operating statements alongside production data.

If you're not sure whether you hold royalty, mineral, or working interest, that's a common question and one we sort out early using your division order or JOA documentation before any pricing conversation.

faqs.q: How do you know if your minerals are on Fort Berthold trust land?
faqs.a: This is established in your title history and, for trust or allotted interests, in Bureau of Indian Affairs records rather than a standard county deed alone. We confirm this early in diligence since it determines the entire transfer process.

faqs.q: Does a trust land sale take longer to close?
faqs.a: Generally yes, since it requires Bureau of Indian Affairs approval in addition to standard title work. We coordinate that process directly and set a realistic timeline from the start rather than promising a standard closing date.

faqs.q: What's the difference between your Middle Bakken and Three Forks interests?
faqs.a: They're separate producing intervals that can be developed by different wells over time, sometimes years apart, under the same spacing unit. We review your full well history to confirm which formations are actually generating your current royalty income.

faqs.q: Is Bakken development still active, or has it slowed like some other shale plays?
faqs.a: Core McKenzie and Mountrail County areas have continued seeing horizontal development, though the pace varies with oil pricing like any basin. We check current permitting and completion activity for your specific tract rather than assuming a constant pace.

faqs.q: How do you know if you hold royalty interest or working interest?
faqs.a: Your division order or, for working interest, a joint operating agreement will specify this. If you're unsure, send us what you have and we'll confirm before discussing pricing.

faqs.q: What if your unit includes both a Fort Berthold trust portion and private minerals?
faqs.a: We confirm the specific status of your individual interest rather than the whole unit, since ownership type is determined tract by tract, not by what else sits inside the same spacing unit.

faqs.q: How often do division orders get corrected in this basin?
faqs.a: Corrections happen periodically as operators refine allocation calculations across multi-well pads. We compare your current statement against the division order specifically to catch any mismatch before closing.

items.name: Marcellus Shale Mineral Rights
items.meta: Selling Marcellus Shale gas minerals in Pennsylvania or West Virginia? Learn how state-specific pooling law and deduction disputes shape the sale.

sections.html:
Pennsylvania and West Virginia handle unleased and fractionally owned Marcellus minerals very differently, so which state your tract sits in changes the title conversation from the start.

The Marcellus Shale underlies a broad footprint across Pennsylvania and West Virginia, and it's been one of the most productive natural gas plays in the country for over a decade, which means most Marcellus tracts we evaluate already have a lease and production history behind them. The purchase process follows the standard sequence of title review, offer, escrow, and closing, but two state-specific legal frameworks deserve real attention: how each state treats forced integration of unleased interests, and how post-production cost deductions have played out in each state's courts.

sections.title: Pennsylvania versus West Virginia pooling and integration law
sections.html: Pennsylvania's ability to force unleased owners into a producing unit is narrower than in many gas states, generally limited to older statutory frameworks that don't apply cleanly to modern horizontal Marcellus units, which means unleased Pennsylvania tracts more often sit outside a unit entirely rather than being pooled into one. West Virginia, by contrast, has co-tenancy and lease integration statutes that allow an operator to develop a tract even when some fractional owners haven't signed a lease, under specific conditions. We confirm which framework applies to your tract and pull the relevant order or agreement before structuring a purchase, since the two states produce very different documentation trails.

sections.title: Post-production deduction disputes and what they mean for your statement
sections.html: Pennsylvania has seen significant litigation and regulatory attention over post-production cost deductions on gas royalty statements, with court decisions affecting how much operators can deduct depending on specific lease language, particularly around older leases that predate current market norms. We review your lease's royalty and deduction clauses against your actual statement during diligence, since a lease with unfavorable deduction language can mean a materially lower net royalty than the same gross production would generate under a cleaner lease.

sections.title: Fractional and split-estate ownership across generations
sections.html: Marcellus tracts, especially in Pennsylvania and northern West Virginia, frequently carry ownership that's been split across generations of heirs, sometimes with the surface owned separately from the minerals going back a century or more. We trace this chain during title review and confirm your specific fractional share against the county record and, where applicable, the operator's division order before making an offer, since older split-estate chains are one of the more common sources of title questions in this play.

sections.title: What we ask for before pricing your interest
sections.html:
A recent royalty statement showing gross value and any deductions, along with the original lease, are the two most useful documents for a Marcellus Shale review, since together they let us assess both your decimal interest and your actual net royalty economics. For West Virginia interests brought into a unit through integration rather than a signed lease, we request that order or agreement directly.

Given how often ownership here has split across generations, we also ask about any known co-owners or family members who may hold a share of the same original interest, since identifying them early keeps a multi-heir sale on schedule.

faqs.q: You never leased your Marcellus minerals. Can they still be developed and can you still sell?
faqs.a: It depends on your state. West Virginia has integration statutes that can bring unleased fractional owners into a unit under specific conditions; Pennsylvania's forced pooling authority is narrower. We confirm your state's applicable framework and your specific status before structuring an offer.

faqs.q: Why does your Pennsylvania royalty check seem lower than expected for the production volume?
faqs.a: Pennsylvania has seen real litigation over post-production deduction practices, and older leases sometimes carry language that allows larger deductions than newer leases. We review your lease terms specifically to understand what's driving your net payment.

faqs.q: Your mineral ownership has been split among many cousins over generations. Is that a problem?
faqs.a: It's common in this play and workable. We trace the full chain of conveyances and heirship to confirm each owner's exact fractional share, and we can work with individual family members who want to sell their portion independently.

faqs.q: Does it matter whether you're in Pennsylvania or West Virginia for how quickly we can close?
faqs.a: It can. The two states' county recording systems and legal frameworks differ, so timelines vary by county more than by a blanket state rule. We scope the specific timeline for your county early in the process.

faqs.q: What if you only hold a small fractional share inherited from a larger family interest?
faqs.a: We regularly purchase individual fractional shares. You don't need other family members to participate for us to buy your specific portion, though coordinating together can sometimes simplify title work.

faqs.q: Can you purchase minerals that are currently unleased?
faqs.a: Yes, we evaluate unleased Marcellus interests as well, pricing against nearby activity and the likelihood of future leasing or integration rather than existing production.

faqs.q: Do older, pre-shale-boom conventional leases still exist in this footprint?
faqs.a: Some tracts carry older conventional leases predating the Marcellus horizontal boom, occasionally with different terms than a modern horizontal lease. We review whichever lease actually governs your interest.

items.name: Utica Shale Mineral Rights
items.meta: Selling Ohio Utica Shale minerals? Learn how the deeper Utica interacts with Marcellus rights above it, plus Ohio's mandatory pooling process.

sections.html:
In parts of eastern Ohio, the same acreage can carry separately valuable Marcellus rights above and Utica rights below, so the first diligence question is which interval your lease actually covers.

The Utica Shale sits beneath the Marcellus across much of eastern Ohio, and while the two formations are sometimes discussed together because they're stacked in the same region, they're separately targeted intervals with their own lease terms, operators, and in some cases separate ownership history. Ohio's Utica development has concentrated in a fairway of counties in the eastern part of the state, with liquids-rich and dry-gas windows behaving differently depending on location, similar in concept to the Eagle Ford's window structure but specific to this play.

The purchase process runs through the standard title, offer, escrow, and closing sequence, with particular attention paid to which formation your lease actually covers and, where relevant, Ohio's mandatory pooling process for unleased owners.

sections.title: Confirming which formation your lease actually covers
sections.html: Some eastern Ohio leases were written broadly enough to cover multiple formations, while others were negotiated or amended specifically for Utica rights after an earlier, separate Marcellus lease. Before structuring an offer, we confirm exactly which depths and formations your specific lease and any amendments cover, since an owner can hold Utica rights, Marcellus rights, or both, with potentially different operators and royalty terms attached to each. This is one of the more common sources of confusion we see in this play, and it's worth clarifying before any valuation conversation.

sections.title: Ohio's mandatory pooling process
sections.html: Ohio allows an operator to apply to the Ohio Department of Natural Resources for a mandatory pooling order that brings unleased or nonconsenting owners into a unit under defined terms, functioning similarly in effect to Oklahoma's forced pooling but administered through a different state agency and process. If your minerals were pooled rather than leased, we pull the ODNR pooling order to confirm your election and current payment status as part of diligence, and we structure the assignment at closing to reference that order alongside the standard deed.

sections.title: Liquids-rich versus dry gas window position
sections.html: The Utica fairway in Ohio has a liquids-rich window, where wells produce meaningful oil and natural gas liquids alongside gas, and a dry gas window further east and south where output is almost entirely gas. This affects royalty character in the same way an oil-versus-gas window distinction does in other plays — liquids-rich production tends to carry different pricing dynamics than dry gas. We check your specific county and production mix as part of valuation rather than assuming uniform behavior across the whole Utica fairway.

sections.title: What we ask for before pricing your interest
sections.html:
A recent royalty statement and the lease or lease amendment specifying which formation depths are covered are the most important documents for a Utica Shale review, since confirming exactly what's leased is often the central question here. For interests brought into a unit through ODNR mandatory pooling rather than a lease, we request that order directly.

If you're unsure whether your documents cover Utica rights, Marcellus rights, or both, we review the language directly rather than assuming, since this is one of the most common points of confusion in this play.

faqs.q: Do you own Marcellus rights, Utica rights, or both?
faqs.a: It depends on the specific depths named in your lease and any amendments. We review the lease language directly rather than assuming based on your county, since ownership of the two formations is sometimes split or covered separately even on the same tract.

faqs.q: You were pooled by an ODNR order rather than a signed lease. Can you still sell?
faqs.a: Yes. We pull the mandatory pooling order to confirm your election and payment terms, and we can purchase the interest with the assignment referencing that order so the operator's records and the county deed record stay consistent.

faqs.q: Is liquids-rich Utica acreage worth more than dry gas Utica acreage?
faqs.a: It depends on current pricing and documented production for your specific tract; liquids-rich production carries different revenue characteristics than dry gas. We evaluate your actual production mix rather than applying a blanket assumption based on general window location.

faqs.q: How mature is Utica Shale development compared to the Marcellus above it?
faqs.a: Utica development in Ohio generally started somewhat later than Marcellus development in Pennsylvania and West Virginia, so some Utica tracts have shorter production histories. We work from whatever current data exists for your specific well or unit.

faqs.q: What if your lease doesn't specify a formation at all?
faqs.a: Older or broadly worded leases sometimes don't name a specific formation. We review the full depth and habendum language to determine what's actually covered before structuring an offer.

faqs.q: Can the same tract have separate Marcellus and Utica leases with different terms?
faqs.a: Yes, this happens when a Marcellus lease was signed first and a separate Utica lease or amendment came later, often with different royalty terms. We review each lease independently.

faqs.q: Do liquids-rich Utica wells decline differently than dry gas Utica wells?
faqs.a: Production character differs somewhat between the two windows, and we evaluate your well's actual documented decline pattern rather than applying a generic Utica-wide assumption.

items.name: DJ Basin Mineral Rights
items.meta: Selling DJ Basin minerals near Colorado's Wattenberg Field? Here's how setback rules, Niobrara/Codell benches, and closing actually work.

sections.html:
Colorado regulates where and how a well can be drilled near homes and schools more tightly than most states, and that overlay shows up directly in DJ Basin diligence.

The Denver-Julesburg Basin centers on the Wattenberg Field in Weld County, Colorado, one of the most densely drilled oil and gas fields in the country, with development also extending into Wyoming and Nebraska on the basin's edges. Most DJ Basin minerals we evaluate already have some production or permitting history, since the core field has been drilled continuously for decades and intensively so over the last ten years with horizontal development.

What sets a DJ Basin purchase apart from other basins isn't the mineral transfer mechanics — those follow the standard title, offer, escrow, closing sequence — it's the regulatory layer around surface access and setbacks that operators have to navigate, which can affect permitting timelines and, in turn, how we assess near-term activity on a specific tract.

sections.title: Setback rules and what they mean for permitting activity
sections.html: Colorado's oil and gas regulator, the Energy and Carbon Management Commission, enforces statewide setback distances between wells and occupied buildings that are stricter than in most producing states, and Weld County's own land use rules add another layer on top. In practice, this means some tracts near residential development have seen permitting slow or shift to different well pad locations than would be typical elsewhere, while rural core-field acreage away from rooftops continues to see active horizontal drilling. We check current permit filings and pad locations for your specific section, since setback exposure varies block by block within the same county.

sections.title: Niobrara and Codell bench activity
sections.html: Wattenberg Field development targets the Niobrara chalk, typically across its A, B, and C benches, along with the Codell sandstone just below it, often in the same multi-well pad. Because this field has been developed in phases over many years, some tracts have older vertical wellbores from decades ago still on the books alongside newer horizontal units, and division orders can reflect both. We review the full well history for your tract, not only the most recent horizontal unit, since older interests sometimes carry different royalty terms that still affect your current statement.

sections.title: Closing and proration on Wattenberg Field interests
sections.html: Weld County's records are well digitized, and most DJ Basin tracts we purchase are already producing, so closing typically includes proration of the most recent royalty check to the exact closing date. Escrow holds the purchase funds until title is confirmed clean and the operator's division order team has what it needs to process the transfer, which for an active Wattenberg tract is usually a straightforward, well-documented process compared to more rural basins.

sections.title: What we ask for before pricing your interest
sections.html:
For a producing Wattenberg Field tract, a recent royalty statement and the current division order let us confirm your decimal interest quickly, since Weld County operators generally maintain well-organized records. For acreage that's leased but not yet producing, we work from the lease and any current permit filings for your section.

If your tract has both older vertical wellbore history and a newer horizontal unit, providing whatever historical statements you have helps us build a complete picture, though we can also reconstruct much of that history directly from operator and county records if your own files are incomplete.

faqs.q: Do Colorado setback rules affect whether your minerals get drilled?
faqs.a: They can affect where and when a well pad is sited near your acreage, particularly close to residential areas, but they don't eliminate development rights. We check current permitting activity for your specific tract rather than assuming setbacks stop drilling outright.

faqs.q: What's the difference between the Niobrara and Codell on your division order?
faqs.a: They're separate producing zones often developed together from the same pad but sometimes carrying different unit configurations or historical lease terms. We review both when they apply to your tract so the offer reflects the full picture, not only the most recent well.

faqs.q: Is Weld County title research faster than other basins?
faqs.a: Generally yes. Weld County's clerk and recorder records are well digitized, which usually keeps title review and closing timelines shorter than basins with more rural, less digitized counties.

faqs.q: Can you sell if your tract has an old vertical well plus a newer horizontal unit?
faqs.a: Yes. We review the complete well history, including legacy vertical wellbores, to make sure the offer accounts for every producing interest tied to your minerals, not only the most recent development.

faqs.q: Does an older vertical well on your tract affect a newer horizontal unit's value?
faqs.a: It can add documentation to review but doesn't reduce value on its own. We check the full well history so the offer reflects everything tied to your minerals.

faqs.q: Do you purchase minerals near residential development where setbacks apply?
faqs.a: Yes. Setback rules affect where a well can be sited, not whether your minerals can be sold. We check current and likely future activity for your specific tract before making an offer.

faqs.q: Does a multi-well pad near your tract change how your interest is valued?
faqs.a: It can, since a densely developed pad often means more completed wells contributing to your unit. We review the full pad history rather than pricing off a single well.

items.name: Niobrara Mineral Rights
items.meta: "Niobrara" spans several basins. Here's how we confirm which one your minerals sit in and how that changes the mineral purchase process.

sections.html:
Niobrara isn't a basin, it's a formation, and it runs under parts of the DJ Basin, the Powder River Basin, and the Piceance Basin, each with a completely different operator and title picture.

It's common for a mineral owner to describe their interest as "Niobrara minerals" because that's the formation name on a division order or a lease, but the Niobrara chalk and shale extend across several separate producing basins in Colorado, Wyoming, and Nebraska. Before we can talk about value or process, the first job is pinning down which basin your specific tract actually sits in, because that determines the operator, the regulatory environment, and the diligence checklist we run.

Once we've confirmed the basin, the purchase follows that basin's normal process — this page exists to walk through how we make that identification and what tends to differ once we know.

sections.title: How we identify which basin your Niobrara minerals sit in
sections.html:
We start with the legal description on your deed or division order and cross-reference the county against known Niobrara-producing basins. Weld County, Colorado and surrounding areas point to the DJ Basin and the Wattenberg Field. Wyoming counties like Converse or Campbell point to the Powder River Basin, where Niobrara horizontal development has grown substantially over the last several years alongside the older Turner sand play. Northwest Colorado counties can point to the Piceance Basin, where Niobrara gas has historically been a secondary target behind the Mesaverde.

This isn't a formality — it changes everything downstream. A DJ Basin Niobrara tract in dense Wattenberg development has a very different activity and title profile than a Powder River Basin Niobrara tract still in earlier-stage horizontal delineation, even though both division orders might say "Niobrara" in the formation field.

sections.title: Why formation-only descriptions cause valuation confusion
sections.html: We regularly hear from owners who compare their offer to a number they saw online for "Niobrara minerals" without realizing that figure applied to a different basin entirely. Activity levels, well density, and operator competition for acreage vary enormously between the core Wattenberg Field and the newer Powder River Basin Niobrara fairway, so a single blended number for "the Niobrara" isn't meaningful. We price against the actual basin, county, and documented activity for your specific tract.

sections.title: What happens after basin identification
sections.html: Once we've confirmed which basin governs your minerals, diligence proceeds under that basin's normal framework — Colorado setback and permitting review for DJ Basin tracts, checkerboard and split-estate confirmation for Powder River Basin tracts, or federal lease overlay checks for Piceance Basin tracts. Escrow, proration, and closing mechanics follow the standard process from there, tailored to whichever basin your interest actually sits in.

sections.title: What we ask for before confirming your basin
sections.html:
The fastest way to confirm which basin governs your Niobrara interest is a copy of your deed or a recent division order, both of which include the legal description and county we use to make the identification. If you only have older documents or none at all, your name and approximate property location are usually enough for us to start the lookup directly through county and operator records.

Once the basin is confirmed, we request whatever additional documentation that basin's process calls for, whether that's a Colorado permit history, a Wyoming lease, or federal record, and walk you through why that basin's specific framework applies to your tract.

faqs.q: Your division order says "Niobrara" — how do you know which basin that means?
faqs.a: The county listed on your deed or division order tells us the basin. We confirm this in the first step of review, since the Niobrara formation crosses the DJ, Powder River, and Piceance Basins with very different activity levels in each.

faqs.q: Does it matter which basin your Niobrara minerals are in for pricing?
faqs.a: Significantly. Well density, operator activity, and recent comparable transactions differ by basin, so we price against your specific basin and county rather than a general "Niobrara" figure, which isn't meaningful across such different areas.

faqs.q: Is Powder River Basin Niobrara development as advanced as the DJ Basin's?
faqs.a: Generally the DJ Basin's Wattenberg Field has a longer, denser development history. Powder River Basin Niobrara horizontal activity has grown substantially in recent years but tract-by-tract activity still varies more than in the mature Wattenberg core.

faqs.q: What if your minerals are under the Niobrara in the Piceance Basin?
faqs.a: Piceance Basin Niobrara gas has historically been a secondary target behind the Mesaverde formation, so activity and diligence there look more like a Piceance Basin gas tract than a DJ Basin oil tract. We assess it under that basin's framework.

faqs.q: What if your documents don't clearly state a county?
faqs.a: We can usually determine your county from a legal description, township and range, or even the operator name on a statement, so incomplete paperwork isn't a barrier to getting started.

faqs.q: What if your legal description spans a county line?
faqs.a: We confirm the operative county from the specific section, township, and range on your document rather than a mailing address, since that's what actually determines the governing basin and jurisdiction.

items.name: Powder River Basin Mineral Rights
items.meta: Selling Wyoming or Montana Powder River Basin minerals? Learn how checkerboard land grants, split estate, and CBM legacy interests shape a sale.

sections.html:
Powder River Basin land ownership still carries the fingerprints of a 19th-century railroad land grant, and that checkerboard pattern shows up directly in how spacing units get built here today.

The Powder River Basin spans northeast Wyoming and southeast Montana, historically known for large-scale coalbed methane development starting in the 1990s and, more recently, for horizontal oil development targeting the Niobrara and Turner sand formations. Because both eras of development sit on the same acreage in many areas, a Powder River Basin mineral owner may hold interests tied to legacy CBM production, newer horizontal oil development, or both, depending on the specific tract and formation.

Ownership patterns here also reflect the basin's history as railroad land grant territory, which created an alternating checkerboard of private, state, and federal minerals that operators have to work around when configuring modern horizontal units.

sections.title: Checkerboard ownership and split estate
sections.html: Much of the Powder River Basin's land pattern traces back to 19th-century railroad grants that awarded alternating sections to the railroad and reserved others for the federal government, a legacy still visible in the mixed private, state, and federal mineral ownership across the basin today. It's also common here for surface and mineral ownership to be split, with a rancher owning the surface while a separate party, sometimes descendants of an earlier owner, holds the minerals. We confirm both the checkerboard unit configuration and the surface-mineral ownership split during diligence, since either can affect access, unit boundaries, and how your specific interest is documented.

sections.title: What we ask for before pricing your interest
sections.html:
A recent royalty statement, or confirmation that a well has been plugged, is the most useful starting point for a legacy CBM interest, while a current division order works best for newer horizontal Niobrara or Turner development. We also ask whether you hold the surface as well as the minerals, since split estate is common here and doesn't affect what we can purchase, but helps us understand the full picture of your ownership.

For tracts touching the basin's checkerboard federal or state sections, we confirm the specific unit configuration directly with BLM or Wyoming state land records as part of standard diligence.

sections.title: Legacy coalbed methane versus newer horizontal oil development
sections.html: CBM development in this basin peaked in the 2000s and has since matured into long, low-decline production on many legacy wells, some of which have reached the end of their economic life and been plugged. More recently, horizontal drilling targeting the Niobrara and Turner formations has brought renewed oil-focused activity to parts of the basin, often on the same acreage that once hosted CBM wells but from separately configured units at different depths. We check which type of development, if any, is currently active on your specific tract, since a legacy CBM interest and a newer horizontal oil interest are different assets with different valuation profiles even on the same land.

sections.title: Title and closing across Campbell and Converse Counties
sections.html: Core Powder River Basin activity concentrates in Wyoming's Campbell and Converse Counties, where county clerk records are generally solid, though the checkerboard ownership pattern means we often cross-reference BLM and Wyoming state land records alongside county deed records to build a complete title picture. Escrow and closing follow the standard sequence once that full chain is confirmed clean.

faqs.q: Why is land ownership so checkerboarded in this basin?
faqs.a: It traces back to 19th-century railroad land grants that alternated sections between the railroad and the federal government, a pattern still reflected in today's mixed private, state, and federal mineral ownership across the Powder River Basin.

faqs.q: You have an old CBM well and you've heard about new horizontal oil wells nearby. Are these the same interest?
faqs.a: Not necessarily. Legacy coalbed methane production and newer horizontal Niobrara or Turner oil development are often configured as separate units at different depths, even on the same acreage. We check which specific development applies to your interest before valuing it.

faqs.q: Is your old CBM well still producing?
faqs.a: Some legacy Powder River Basin CBM wells continue producing at mature, low-decline levels; others have reached the end of their economic life and been plugged. We confirm current status directly for your specific well as part of diligence.

faqs.q: Do you need to own the surface to sell your minerals here?
faqs.a: No. Split estate, where the surface and minerals are owned separately, is common in this basin, and we regularly purchase mineral interests where the seller has no surface ownership at all.

faqs.q: Does not owning the surface limit what you can sell?
faqs.a: No. Split estate ownership is common in this basin, and we regularly purchase mineral interests from owners who hold no surface rights at all.

faqs.q: How does the closing desk determine which formation an owner's interest is tied to?
faqs.a: We review the specific well or unit documentation, including depth and formation names in the division order or lease, rather than assuming based on the general area's development history.

faqs.q: Is Converse County seeing more current activity than Campbell County?
