faqs.a: Recent horizontal Niobrara and Turner development has been notable in Converse County specifically, though Campbell County retains substantial legacy CBM production. We check your specific tract's status either way.

items.name: San Juan Basin Mineral Rights
items.meta: Selling New Mexico or Colorado San Juan Basin minerals? Learn how mature CBM production and Navajo Nation allotted land affect a purchase.

sections.html:
Parts of the San Juan Basin overlap Navajo Nation allotted lands, and where that's the case, a mineral transfer runs through Bureau of Indian Affairs approval rather than the county clerk alone.

The San Juan Basin, spanning northwest New Mexico and southwest Colorado, is one of the country's oldest and most mature natural gas basins, with development stretching back to the 1950s and expanding significantly through coalbed methane production in the 1980s and 1990s. Most tracts we evaluate here have decades of production history behind them, and ownership can range from straightforward private fee minerals to interests tied to allotted trust land within the Navajo Nation, which follow an entirely different transfer process.

The core purchase steps are the same as any basin, but San Juan Basin diligence starts with confirming what type of ownership you actually hold, since that determines which agencies and records govern the transfer.

sections.title: Fee minerals versus Navajo Nation allotted trust land
sections.html: If your minerals are private fee ownership, meaning they trace through a standard chain of deeds outside any tribal trust status, the purchase follows the normal county-based process. If your interest is instead an allotted trust interest tied to Navajo Nation land, any transfer requires approval through the Bureau of Indian Affairs rather than a simple county deed recording, and the timeline and documentation requirements are materially different. We confirm which category applies to your specific interest at the very start of diligence, since it changes the entire process from there forward.

sections.title: What we ask for before pricing your interest
sections.html:
For fee mineral interests, a recent royalty statement and the original lease or deed are the key documents we start with. For allotted trust interests, we instead work primarily from Bureau of Indian Affairs records, and we'll walk you through exactly what documentation that process requires, since it differs meaningfully from a standard county-based sale.

Given how many San Juan Basin interests have passed through multiple generations, we also commonly help coordinate a sale across several heirs who each hold a fractional share of the same original interest.

sections.title: Mature CBM and conventional gas production
sections.html: San Juan Basin gas production spans both older conventional wells from the mid-20th century and coalbed methane wells from the later boom, and many tracts have both types of production history layered on the same or adjacent acreage. Decades in, most wells here have settled into long, low-decline production, and we evaluate current, documented output for your specific tract rather than the basin's historical peak output from its more active development decades.

sections.title: Title review across decades of San Juan Basin leasing
sections.html: Because leasing here began generations ago in some areas, title chains commonly run through multiple rounds of inheritance, and New Mexico and Colorado county records in core counties like San Juan and La Plata require careful chain-of-title work to confirm current ownership accurately. We handle that research directly, and for any interest touching allotted trust land, we coordinate the BIA approval process as part of getting to a clean closing.

faqs.q: How do you know if your minerals are fee ownership or Navajo Nation allotted trust land?
faqs.a: This is typically documented in your original conveyance or, for trust interests, through Bureau of Indian Affairs records rather than a standard county deed. We confirm this early in diligence since it determines the entire transfer process.

faqs.q: Does selling an allotted trust interest take longer than a standard sale?
faqs.a: Generally yes, since it requires Bureau of Indian Affairs approval in addition to standard title work. We coordinate that process directly and build the realistic timeline into the transaction from the start.

faqs.q: Is your San Juan Basin well too old to still be producing?
faqs.a: Many San Juan Basin wells, including decades-old conventional and CBM wells, continue producing at mature, low-decline levels. We check current, documented production for your specific well before valuing the interest.

faqs.q: Can you buy a fractional interest that's been split among many heirs over decades?
faqs.a: Yes. We regularly trace multi-generation heirship chains in this basin and can work with individual heirs who want to sell their specific fractional share.

faqs.q: Can multiple heirs sell their shares of the same interest separately?
faqs.a: Yes, we can work with individual heirs on their specific fractional shares, whether or not other family members choose to sell at the same time.

faqs.q: What if you only recently learned you inherited a San Juan Basin interest?
faqs.a: That's common, and we can help you get oriented, starting with confirming whether the interest is fee or trust land and pulling the current operator and production record from there.

faqs.q: Do you buy interests where production has been essentially flat for years?
faqs.a: Yes, a long, flat, low-decline production profile is typical and expected for mature San Juan Basin wells, and we price against that documented, stable pattern rather than treating it as a red flag.

faqs.q: Does the closing desk handle Bureau of Indian Affairs paperwork for a trust interest?
faqs.a: Yes, we coordinate the required BIA documentation and approval steps directly as part of the transaction, walking you through what's needed rather than leaving you to manage that process alone.

items.name: Piceance Basin Mineral Rights
items.meta: Selling Colorado Piceance Basin tight gas minerals? Honest guidance on quieted activity since the late-2000s gas glut and how a sale works.

sections.html:
Piceance Basin drilling slowed sharply after the late-2000s natural gas price collapse, and an honest read of current activity is more useful here than relying on the basin's earlier reputation.

The Piceance Basin in northwest Colorado holds one of the country's largest tight gas resources in the Mesaverde formation, developed intensively through the mid-2000s before falling natural gas prices made much of that development uneconomic and activity slowed considerably. Some Piceance tracts still have production from wells drilled during that earlier active period, while large areas of the basin have seen little to no new drilling in recent years.

For a mineral owner here, the purchase process is standard, but the valuation conversation depends heavily on an honest look at your specific tract's current status rather than the basin's more active history from over a decade ago.

sections.title: What current Piceance Basin activity actually looks like
sections.html: Federal land makes up a substantial portion of the Piceance Basin's mineral base, and BLM leasing activity here has been more muted in recent years compared to the mid-2000s peak, with natural gas pricing remaining the central factor in whether operators pursue new drilling in a tight gas basin with meaningful well costs. We check current permitting, and specifically whether the well or unit tied to your minerals is still actively producing, shut in, or otherwise quiet, since this basin has more variability in current status than more consistently active plays.

sections.title: Mesaverde production history and long-term decline
sections.html: Wells targeting the Mesaverde in this basin were often drilled in dense patterns during the 2000s boom, and many have now settled into a long, low-decline production tail typical of mature tight gas wells. We evaluate your well's actual current production against its full history, since a tract with a well still producing steadily from that earlier development wave can still represent real, though modest, ongoing value.

sections.title: Title review in Garfield and Rio Blanco Counties
sections.html: Core Piceance Basin counties, Garfield and Rio Blanco, have reasonably maintained county clerk records, and because much of the basin's leasing activity concentrated in a specific window in the 2000s, title chains are moderately aged but generally traceable. We confirm the chain of title and current lease status as part of standard diligence, being upfront if a specific tract's activity level is limited before structuring an offer.

sections.title: What we ask for before pricing your interest
sections.html:
A recent royalty statement, where one exists, tells us the most about a Piceance Basin tract's current status, since activity here varies more than in steadier basins. If your well has gone quiet or you're unsure of its current status, we can check directly with the operator or Colorado's oil and gas regulator rather than requiring you to track that down yourself.

We also review the original lease terms, since older Piceance leases sometimes include shut-in royalty provisions relevant to tracts that have seen reduced activity since the basin's mid-2000s peak.

faqs.q: Is the Piceance Basin still an active gas play?
faqs.a: Activity has been notably quieter since the late-2000s natural gas price decline made much of the basin's tight gas development less economic. Some areas still have producing legacy wells; others have seen little recent activity. We check your specific tract's current status directly.

faqs.q: Why did Piceance Basin drilling slow down so much?
faqs.a: A sharp decline in natural gas prices after the mid-2000s development peak made much of the basin's higher-cost tight gas drilling less attractive relative to other basins, and activity has remained comparatively muted since. This is a documented, basin-wide pattern, not specific to your tract.

faqs.q: Is your mineral interest still worth anything if there hasn't been new drilling recently?
faqs.a: If your tract has an existing producing well, it can still generate steady, if modest, income from that legacy production even without new drilling nearby. We evaluate current, documented production for your specific well before making an offer.

faqs.q: Does federal BLM leasing affect your private minerals here?
faqs.a: It can affect unit configuration if your tract is near or checkerboarded with federal leasehold, similar to other Rocky Mountain basins, though it doesn't change your underlying ownership. We confirm this during diligence.

faqs.q: How do you find out if your well is still active?
faqs.a: We check directly with the operator and Colorado regulatory records as part of diligence, so you don't need to track this down yourself before reaching out.

faqs.q: Do you buy minerals in areas with no recent drilling activity at all?
faqs.a: Yes, we still evaluate these tracts, particularly if there's existing legacy production or lease activity to review, and we're direct about how limited current activity affects the offer.

faqs.q: Would the closing desk contact an owner if activity picked up after a sale?
faqs.a: Once a sale closes, the interest and any future activity belong to the buyer. That's worth weighing carefully, which is why we encourage sellers to ask questions before closing, not after.

faqs.q: Should you expect a slower response given this basin's quieter activity?
faqs.a: No, our review timeline is similar regardless of basin activity level. A quieter basin simply means the offer reflects more modest current production, not a slower process to get there.

items.name: Uinta Basin Mineral Rights
items.meta: Selling Utah Uinta Basin minerals? Learn how waxy crude logistics, federal and Ute tribal minerals, and horizontal development affect a sale.

sections.html:
Uinta Basin crude is thick enough to need special handling just to move it to market, and that logistics reality has shaped how development here has unfolded more than in most basins.

The Uinta Basin in northeast Utah produces a distinctive waxy crude oil that solidifies at relatively warm temperatures, historically requiring heated pipelines, rail transport, or trucking to move to refining markets, a logistics constraint that has shaped the pace of development here differently than in basins with easier takeaway access. Mineral ownership in the basin is a mix of private fee minerals, federal BLM leasehold, and Ute Indian Tribe trust lands, and more recent horizontal drilling in the Uteland Butte and other formations has brought renewed activity after a quieter period.

For a mineral owner, the purchase process depends first on confirming which of those ownership categories applies to your tract, since federal and tribal trust interests follow different transfer processes than private fee minerals.

sections.title: Federal, tribal, and private mineral ownership
sections.html: A meaningful share of Uinta Basin minerals sit on federal BLM leasehold or within Ute Indian Tribe trust land, and transfers involving tribal trust interests require Bureau of Indian Affairs approval rather than a standard county deed recording, similar in process to other basins with tribal trust ownership. Private fee mineral tracts follow the normal county-based title process. We confirm which category governs your specific interest at the outset of diligence, since it determines the entire documentation and approval path from there.

sections.title: Waxy crude logistics and what that means for activity
sections.html: Because Uinta Basin crude requires special handling to transport, takeaway capacity and rail or trucking logistics have historically been a bigger factor in development pace here than in basins with straightforward pipeline access, and periods of tighter logistics capacity have coincided with slower drilling activity. More recently, horizontal development targeting the Uteland Butte and other stacked intervals has brought renewed interest to parts of the basin. We check current permitting and completion activity for your specific tract rather than assuming a constant pace, since this basin's development has moved in more visible cycles tied partly to logistics as well as pricing.

sections.title: Title and closing across Uintah and Duchesne Counties
sections.html: Core Uinta Basin activity concentrates in Uintah and Duchesne Counties, where county clerk records handle private fee mineral chains in the standard way, while any tribal trust or federal leasehold portion of your interest requires the additional coordination described above. We build the realistic timeline for your specific ownership type into the closing schedule from the start, since a straightforward fee mineral sale here can move at a normal pace while a trust interest transfer takes longer by nature.

sections.title: What we ask for before pricing your interest
sections.html:
For private fee mineral interests, a recent royalty statement and division order are the key starting documents. For interests touching Ute Indian Tribe trust land or federal BLM leasehold, we work primarily from Bureau of Indian Affairs or BLM records and will walk you through the specific documentation that process requires.

We also confirm current activity status directly with the operator or Utah's oil and gas regulator, since this basin's development pace has moved in visible cycles tied to both pricing and crude transport logistics.

faqs.q: Why does Uinta Basin oil need special transport?
faqs.a: It's a waxy crude that solidifies at relatively warm temperatures compared to most crude oil, historically requiring heated pipelines, rail, or trucking rather than standard ambient pipeline transport. This has been a real factor in the pace of the basin's development.

faqs.q: Are your minerals private, federal, or Ute Tribe trust land?
faqs.a: This is established in your title history and, for trust interests, in Bureau of Indian Affairs records. We confirm which category applies to your specific tract at the start of diligence, since it determines the entire transfer process.

faqs.q: Does a tribal trust interest take longer to sell than a private mineral interest?
faqs.a: Generally yes, since it requires Bureau of Indian Affairs approval in addition to standard title work. We coordinate that process directly and set realistic expectations on timeline from the outset.

faqs.q: Is the Uinta Basin seeing new drilling activity right now?
faqs.a: Horizontal development targeting the Uteland Butte and other stacked intervals has brought renewed activity to parts of the basin after quieter periods tied to takeaway logistics and pricing. We check current permitting for your specific tract rather than generalizing across the whole basin.

faqs.q: Do you purchase interests involving Ute Tribe trust land?
faqs.a: Yes, though the process runs through Bureau of Indian Affairs approval rather than a standard county closing, and we coordinate that directly with you.

faqs.q: Does waxy crude transport affect the value of your minerals directly?
faqs.a: It affects operator development pace and economics more than it directly changes your ownership value, though we do factor current takeaway conditions into our read of near-term activity for your tract.

faqs.q: Is Duchesne County or Uintah County seeing more current drilling?
faqs.a: Both counties have seen renewed horizontal activity in recent years, with the specific pace varying by operator and formation target. We check current permitting for your exact tract.

items.name: Green River Basin Mineral Rights
items.meta: Selling Wyoming Green River Basin minerals near Pinedale or Jonah Field? Learn how federal BLM leasing and tight gas activity shape a sale.

sections.html:
A large share of Green River Basin mineral acreage sits alongside or checkerboarded with federal land managed by the Bureau of Land Management, and that overlay affects how a unit gets configured around your tract.

The Green River Basin in southwest Wyoming is one of the country's major tight gas basins, home to the Pinedale and Jonah fields, developed through extensive, closely spaced drilling over the past two decades. Federal mineral ownership plays a large role here, with BLM-administered leases interspersed among private and state minerals in many areas, a pattern rooted in historic railroad land grants that created the checkerboard ownership common across the American West.

For a private mineral owner in this basin, that federal overlay doesn't change your ownership, but it does affect how spacing units get configured and what documentation we check during diligence.

sections.title: Checkerboard ownership and unit configuration
sections.html: Historic railroad land grants left much of the Green River Basin in an alternating pattern of federal and private sections, and when an operator builds a horizontal spacing unit today, it often crosses both federal BLM leasehold and private minerals within the same unit. We confirm how your tract's unit is configured, including whether federal leasing terms apply to any portion of the unit, since federal lease royalty and reporting rules differ somewhat from private lease terms and can affect how the overall unit's production is allocated.

sections.title: What we ask for before pricing your interest
sections.html:
A recent royalty statement and division order let us confirm your decimal interest against the current spacing unit configuration, including whether any portion of that unit involves federal BLM leasehold. If your tract has been leased but isn't yet producing, we work from the lease and any BLM or state permitting records tied to your section instead.

We're also glad to walk through how the checkerboard pattern specifically affects your tract, since it's one of the more commonly misunderstood aspects of owning minerals in this basin and worth understanding before you evaluate any offer.

sections.title: Tight gas development in Pinedale and Jonah fields
sections.html: The Pinedale Anticline and Jonah Field have been developed with some of the tightest well spacing in the country, targeting the Lance and Mesaverde formations, and both fields have long, well-documented production histories at this point. We review current well density and production data for your specific tract, since these fields have been developed in phases over many years and activity levels vary depending on where within the field your acreage sits.

sections.title: Title and closing on Sublette and Sweetwater County tracts
sections.html: Core Green River Basin activity concentrates in Sublette and Sweetwater Counties, where county clerk records are generally organized but where the mixed federal, state, and private mineral pattern means title work often involves cross-referencing BLM records alongside county deed records. We handle that cross-referencing directly during diligence and structure escrow and closing around confirmed, clean title, consistent with how we close in any basin.

faqs.q: Does bordering federal BLM land affect your private mineral ownership?
faqs.a: No, it doesn't change your ownership, but it can affect how a spacing unit is configured if your tract borders or is checkerboarded with federal leasehold. We confirm unit configuration during diligence so you understand exactly what's being priced.

faqs.q: Is Pinedale and Jonah Field development still active?
faqs.a: Both fields have long development histories with production still ongoing, though the pace of new drilling has varied over the years. We check current activity for your specific tract rather than assuming a constant development pace across the whole field.

faqs.q: Why is there a mix of federal and private minerals in your area?
faqs.a: This traces back to historic railroad land grants that created an alternating, checkerboard pattern of federal and private land across much of the American West, including the Green River Basin. It's a common historical feature of this region, not anything unusual about your specific tract.

faqs.q: Does federal lease involvement slow down closing?
faqs.a: It can add a documentation step if your unit includes federal leasehold, since we cross-reference BLM records alongside county records. We scope this into the closing timeline upfront so it doesn't create a late surprise.

faqs.q: Do you buy minerals that border but aren't inside federal land?
faqs.a: Yes. Bordering federal land doesn't change your private ownership, though we do confirm how nearby BLM leasehold affects any unit your tract might be included in.

faqs.q: Does state trust land nearby affect your private minerals the same way federal land does?
faqs.a: Wyoming state trust land can similarly factor into unit configuration alongside federal and private minerals, and we confirm whichever combination applies to your specific tract during diligence.

faqs.q: Is Sublette County or Sweetwater County more active right now?
faqs.a: Activity levels shift over time in both counties depending on pricing and operator focus. We check current permitting and production for your specific tract rather than generalizing by county.

faqs.q: Do you buy interests with only partial, older production records available?
faqs.a: Yes, we can reconstruct most of a well's current production picture directly from Wyoming state and operator records, so an incomplete personal file isn't a barrier to getting an offer.

items.name: Smackover Formation Mineral Rights
items.meta: Selling Arkansas or Louisiana Smackover Formation minerals? Learn how legacy oil production and new lithium brine interest affect a sale.

sections.html:
South Arkansas's Smackover Formation is seeing renewed attention for something other than oil, and if your minerals are in the right county, brine rights could matter as much as the traditional oil and gas estate.

The Smackover Formation, spanning parts of south Arkansas and north Louisiana, is one of the oldest producing oil and gas trends in the country, with development dating back nearly a century in some fields. Most Smackover mineral interests we evaluate today are legacy interests under long-established leases, producing at mature, low-decline volumes from conventional oil and gas wells. What's changed more recently is renewed industry interest in the same formation's brine, which carries dissolved lithium in commercially significant concentrations in parts of south Arkansas, drawing new investment into a formation many assumed was purely a legacy oil play.

For a seller, the standard oil and gas mineral purchase process applies to your traditional interest, but if you're in one of the counties where lithium brine development is advancing, it's worth understanding how that ownership question is treated separately.

sections.title: Legacy oil and gas production and long-tail decline
sections.html: Much of the Smackover's traditional oil and gas production comes from fields developed decades ago, and wells here have generally settled into a long, gradually declining production pattern typical of mature conventional reservoirs rather than the steep early decline seen in newer shale plays. We evaluate current, documented production for your specific well or unit, since a legacy Smackover interest with decades of production history is a very different asset to price than a newly permitted tract, even within the same formation.

sections.title: What we ask for before pricing your interest
sections.html:
For a legacy oil and gas interest, a recent royalty statement and the original lease are the key documents, and given how old some Smackover leases are, we're prepared to trace title independently through county and parish records if your own file is incomplete. For owners in counties with active lithium brine development, we also review the specific deed and lease language addressing brine and dissolved minerals as a separate step.

If you're unsure whether your documents address brine rights at all, that's common for older Smackover leases written before brine had any commercial value, and we'll flag it directly rather than assuming either way.

sections.title: Lithium brine and how that ownership question is handled
sections.html: In parts of south Arkansas, particularly Columbia, Union, and Lafayette Counties, the Smackover's brine has drawn significant new investment for lithium extraction, separate from the formation's traditional oil and gas production. Whether brine or specific dissolved minerals within it are covered by your existing oil and gas mineral rights, versus requiring a separate brine or mineral lease, depends on the specific language in your deed and lease and can vary by tract. We review this distinction directly for owners in the relevant counties, since it's a live and evolving area rather than settled, uniform practice, and we're upfront when a specific brine ownership question needs closer legal review before a sale.

sections.title: Title review across a century of Arkansas and Louisiana leasing
sections.html: Because Smackover leasing in some fields dates back to the early-to-mid 20th century, title chains here can be some of the longest and most layered we review, often including multiple generations of heirship, older probate records, and historical severances of oil and gas from other mineral rights. We trace this full history during diligence in the relevant Arkansas and Louisiana parish and county records before structuring any offer.

faqs.q: Do you automatically own lithium brine rights if you own oil and gas minerals in this formation?
faqs.a: Not necessarily. Whether brine and its dissolved minerals fall under your existing oil and gas rights or require separate treatment depends on your specific deed and lease language, and this is still an evolving area in parts of Arkansas. We review your documents directly rather than assuming either way.

faqs.q: Is your old Smackover well still worth selling if it's been producing for decades?
faqs.a: Yes. Mature, long-tail conventional production is still a real income-generating interest, and we price it based on current, documented output rather than the well's original decades-old peak.

faqs.q: Which counties have active lithium brine development in the Smackover?
faqs.a: South Arkansas counties including Columbia, Union, and Lafayette have seen the most active recent investment in Smackover brine and lithium development, though this is an evolving area and activity can shift. We check current status for your specific location.

faqs.q: Can you sell your traditional oil and gas rights separately from any brine interest?
faqs.a: In many cases yes, since these can be distinct rights depending on your deed language. We review your specific documents to clarify what's being sold before structuring any offer.

faqs.q: Can the closing desk confirm whether an owner holds brine rights before a sale?
faqs.a: We review your specific deed and lease language and give you a direct answer on what our review found, rather than leaving that ambiguous.

faqs.q: What if your tract is outside the counties seeing lithium brine investment?
faqs.a: Then your interest is evaluated purely as a traditional oil and gas mineral interest, priced against your well's documented current production, with no brine-related considerations affecting the review.

items.name: Tuscaloosa Marine Shale Mineral Rights
items.meta: Selling Louisiana or Mississippi Tuscaloosa Marine Shale minerals? Honest guidance on this stalled play's legacy leases and how a sale works.

sections.html:
The Tuscaloosa Marine Shale drew heavy leasing activity between 2010 and 2014 that mostly didn't turn into lasting production, and an honest accounting of that is the right place to start.

The Tuscaloosa Marine Shale underlies parts of southern Louisiana and southwest Mississippi, and it was leased aggressively during the broader shale land rush of the early 2010s on the expectation that horizontal drilling techniques proven elsewhere would work here too. In practice, well costs and completion challenges specific to this formation made much of that early drilling uneconomic, and development largely stalled well before the play reached the scale seen in other major shale basins. Today, most Tuscaloosa Marine Shale mineral interests we evaluate are under leases from that 2010 to 2014 window, many with limited or no current production.

We think it's important to be direct about that history upfront, because a fair valuation here depends on an honest read of your specific lease and tract status rather than expectations set by the play's early promotional period.

sections.title: Why this play stalled and what that means today
sections.html: The Tuscaloosa Marine Shale's rock characteristics made horizontal completions more difficult and expensive relative to other contemporaneous shale plays, and as drilling results came in below expectations, operator activity slowed sharply after the initial 2010 to 2014 leasing and early drilling wave. Some wells were drilled and produced for a period; a larger share of leased acreage across the play saw no drilling at all. We check the specific status of your tract directly, since outcomes vary significantly even within the same play.

sections.title: Lease status on non-producing acreage
sections.html: If your minerals were leased during the original boom but no well was ever drilled on your specific tract, the lease's primary term and any extension or delay rental provisions determine whether it's still in effect or has expired back to you. We review the lease terms and, where possible, confirm current status with available records, since an expired lease actually simplifies a sale in some respects — it means there's no existing operator relationship to account for, just a clean mineral interest.

sections.title: Title review across Louisiana and Mississippi
sections.html: Core Tuscaloosa Marine Shale counties and parishes, including St. Helena, East Feliciana, and Wilkinson County across the state line, saw a wave of lease acquisitions during the boom years that sometimes complicated older title chains with new instruments. We work through this directly during diligence, confirming what's current, what's expired, and what your clean, sellable interest actually looks like today.

sections.title: What we ask for before pricing your interest
sections.html:
The original lease from the 2010 to 2014 leasing wave is the most important document for a Tuscaloosa Marine Shale review, since its primary term and extension provisions determine whether it's still in effect. If you're not sure whether your lease is still active, we can check the well or unit status directly through Louisiana and Mississippi regulatory records rather than requiring you to determine that yourself.

For tracts where no well was ever drilled, confirming lease status is really the whole diligence process, after which pricing reflects your clean, unencumbered mineral interest.

faqs.q: Is the Tuscaloosa Marine Shale still being developed?
faqs.a: Activity slowed sharply after the initial 2010 to 2014 leasing and drilling wave produced disappointing results relative to well costs. Some legacy production continues on tracts that were drilled; much of the play saw limited or no drilling. We check your specific tract's status directly.

faqs.q: Your minerals were leased years ago but no well was ever drilled. Is the lease still active?
faqs.a: It depends on the lease's primary term and any extension provisions. Many leases from this play's boom years have since expired without a well being drilled, which we confirm during diligence; an expired lease can actually simplify your sale.

faqs.q: Is your mineral interest worth anything if there's no current production?
faqs.a: Non-producing minerals still have value, particularly if the lease has expired and you hold a clean, unencumbered interest. Valuation reflects the tract's actual status rather than a blanket assumption based on the play's disappointing overall history.

faqs.q: Why did this play not develop the way other shale plays did?
faqs.a: The formation's specific rock characteristics made horizontal completions more difficult and expensive here than in some other contemporaneous plays, and results came in below what the initial leasing wave anticipated. This is a documented, play-wide pattern rather than something specific to any one tract.

faqs.q: Will the closing desk state plainly whether a lease has expired?
faqs.a: Yes, we check the lease's terms against the well or unit's actual history and give you a straightforward answer rather than an ambiguous one.

faqs.q: Will an expired lease need to be cleaned up before you sell?
faqs.a: Generally not from your side. We confirm the lease has lapsed as part of diligence and structure the purchase around your clean, currently unencumbered mineral interest.

faqs.q: Could this play see renewed development in the future?
faqs.a: It's possible if well costs or commodity pricing shift favorably, though nothing currently indicates an imminent change. We price based on documented current status, not speculation about future development.

items.name: Antrim Shale Mineral Rights
items.meta: Selling Michigan Antrim Shale minerals? A straightforward look at this decades-old biogenic gas play, legacy leases, and how a sale works.

sections.html:
Antrim Shale wells were mostly drilled in the 1980s and 1990s, so if you're holding minerals in this play, you're almost certainly dealing with a lease and a well older than most other plays we work with.

The Antrim Shale, centered in Michigan's northern Lower Peninsula, produces biogenic natural gas from a shallow formation that was developed heavily in the 1980s and 1990s, well before the modern horizontal shale boom in other basins. That timing shapes almost everything about a purchase here: wells are old, decline curves settled into their long-term pattern decades ago, and title chains have often passed through multiple generations since the original lease was signed.

This is a quieter, more stable corner of the mineral rights market than newer shale plays, and we approach it that way — grounded in the well's actual current production and a careful title review rather than speculation about new drilling.

sections.title: Shallow, biogenic gas and stable long-term decline
sections.html: Unlike thermogenic shale gas formed under high heat and pressure at depth, Antrim Shale gas is largely biogenic, generated by microbial activity at relatively shallow depths, which gives these wells a different production character than deeper shale plays — generally lower initial rates but a long, gradually declining tail that many wells have sustained for two or three decades. We review your well's specific production history against this long-term pattern to understand what income level is realistic going forward, rather than comparing it to steeper-decline plays elsewhere.

sections.title: Legacy lease terms from an earlier era of gas development
sections.html: Leases in this play typically predate the more standardized post-production deduction language common in leases signed during the 2000s and 2010s shale boom, which means Antrim leases can have simpler, sometimes more favorable royalty terms, though every lease is different and needs individual review. We pull the original lease and any amendments during diligence to confirm exactly what royalty terms currently govern your interest before structuring an offer.

sections.title: Multi-generation title chains in northern Michigan counties
sections.html: Given that most active leases here are thirty to forty years old, it's common for the current owner to be a grandchild or great-grandchild of the person who originally signed. We trace the full chain of conveyances and any probate or heirship documentation through Michigan county records in the core Antrim counties like Otsego, Antrim, and Otsego, confirming your exact fractional share before we make an offer.

sections.title: What to gather before we start a review
sections.html:
A current or recent royalty statement is the most useful starting point, since it confirms which operator and well your interest is tied to and gives us a baseline production figure. If you don't have a recent statement, we can typically identify the correct operator using your county and legal description and request current status directly.

We also ask whether you're aware of any other family members who share the same original mineral interest, since Antrim Shale ownership is so often split across a family. Identifying co-owners early avoids delays later in the title process if a sale needs to close on multiple fractional shares at once.

faqs.q: Is the Antrim Shale still producing after all these years?
faqs.a: Many Antrim wells continue producing at low, stable volumes decades after initial completion, reflecting the play's characteristic long, gradual decline. We check your specific well's current production as part of diligence rather than assuming it's stopped simply because of the play's age.

faqs.q: How do you find your original family lease if it's decades old?
faqs.a: We can typically retrieve lease and conveyance documents directly from county clerk records even for older Antrim leases, so you don't necessarily need to locate original paper copies yourself.

faqs.q: Your grandparent originally signed the lease. How do you prove you now own the interest?
faqs.a: We'll need documentation showing how the interest passed to you, such as probate records, a will, or an affidavit of heirship, which we help identify and gather as part of the title review before closing.

faqs.q: Are Antrim Shale royalty terms different from newer shale leases?
faqs.a: Often, yes. Because these leases predate more recent, deduction-heavy standard language, some Antrim leases carry simpler royalty terms, though this varies by lease and needs individual confirmation, which we handle during diligence.

faqs.q: Do you need the original 1980s or 1990s lease document to sell?
faqs.a: No, we can retrieve it from county records if you don't have your own copy. A recent statement or even just your legal description is enough to start.

faqs.q: Does it matter that the well on your tract is one of the older, original 1980s wells?
faqs.a: Not for whether we'll buy it. We evaluate current documented production regardless of when the well was originally drilled, and many original-era Antrim wells are still steadily producing today.

faqs.q: Do you buy interests where the well has been temporarily shut in?
faqs.a: Yes, a temporary shut-in doesn't disqualify a tract. We check the reason and expected duration as part of confirming current status before structuring an offer.

faqs.q: Can you buy an interest even if the operator has changed hands over the decades?
faqs.a: Yes, operator changes are common over a well's multi-decade life in this play. We confirm the current operator directly from recent statements or state production records before pricing.

items.name: Black Warrior Basin Mineral Rights
items.meta: Selling Alabama Black Warrior Basin coalbed methane minerals? Learn how CBM gas ownership questions and mature production affect a sale.

sections.html:
In coalbed methane country, the gas rights and the coal rights aren't always owned by the same party, and that split is one of the first things we check on a Black Warrior Basin tract.

The Black Warrior Basin in west-central Alabama was one of the pioneering coalbed methane, or CBM, plays in the country, developed heavily starting in the 1980s, producing natural gas from coal seams rather than conventional or shale reservoirs. It's a mature basin today, with most wells decades into a long production life, and ownership here carries a specific complexity worth understanding before any purchase: gas produced from coal seams has, in various instances, been treated as belonging to the coal estate rather than the traditional oil and gas mineral estate, depending on how older conveyances were worded.

That ownership question, along with the basin's long production maturity, shapes how we approach diligence here more than anything else.

sections.title: Why coal ownership and CBM gas ownership can be separate
sections.html: Where land was historically conveyed with the coal reserved separately from the oil and gas, older deed language sometimes didn't clearly address who owns methane gas contained within the coal seam itself, since coalbed methane wasn't a commercially produced resource when many of those older reservations were written. This has been the subject of real legal dispute in coal-producing regions, and the outcome can depend heavily on the specific wording of a decades-old deed. Before we make an offer on a Black Warrior Basin interest, we review the relevant conveyance history to confirm whether you hold the CBM gas rights clearly or whether that ownership needs closer legal review.

sections.title: Mature production and water handling considerations
sections.html: CBM wells typically require dewatering the coal seam before gas flow ramps up, so early production often shows an unusual curve — rising gas output as water production declines, rather than the immediate peak-then-decline pattern typical of conventional or shale oil wells. Decades into this basin's development, most wells have long since passed that dewatering phase and settled into a mature, low-decline production tail. We evaluate your well's current, settled production level directly rather than comparing it to the ramp-up curve from decades ago.

sections.title: Title review across Alabama's coal and mineral history
sections.html: Alabama counties in the Black Warrior Basin, including Tuscaloosa, Jefferson, and Walker, have title histories that often reach back to early 20th-century coal and timber land transactions, layered with later oil and gas leasing. We trace this full chain during diligence, paying particular attention to any severance language distinguishing coal, oil and gas, and CBM rights, since getting this wrong is one of the more consequential mistakes possible in this specific basin.

sections.title: What we review before pricing a CBM interest
sections.html:
Beyond the standard deed and lease chain, a Black Warrior Basin review includes a specific look at how the original severance deed treated coal, oil and gas, and any gas associated with the coal seam, since this is the detail that determines whether you clearly hold the CBM gas rights. We also pull current production data directly from the operator or state records to confirm the well's settled, mature output.

If a severance deed's language is ambiguous about CBM gas ownership, we're upfront about that rather than pricing around it, and we can discuss what additional confirmation, such as a title opinion, might be worth obtaining before a sale closes.

faqs.q: Do you own the gas rights if your family only kept the oil and gas estate, not the coal?
faqs.a: It depends on the specific language in the original severance deed, since coalbed methane ownership has been treated differently than conventional oil and gas rights in some older Alabama conveyances. We review your deed history closely before confirming what you actually hold.

faqs.q: Is your well still worth anything if it was drilled decades ago?
faqs.a: Many Black Warrior Basin CBM wells continue producing at mature, stable levels long after their initial dewatering phase. We evaluate current production directly rather than assuming an old well is no longer productive.

faqs.q: Why did your well's gas production increase for a while after it started, instead of declining right away?
faqs.a: This is a normal characteristic of coalbed methane wells, which need to dewater the coal seam before gas flow builds. If your well is decades old, it has almost certainly moved well past that phase into its long-term production pattern.

faqs.q: What Alabama counties are part of this basin?
faqs.a: Core Black Warrior Basin CBM development centers on counties including Tuscaloosa, Jefferson, and Walker in west-central Alabama, though we confirm activity and title specifics for your exact tract rather than generalizing across the basin.

faqs.q: What if your severance deed language on CBM gas is unclear?
faqs.a: We're upfront if additional confirmation is needed before a sale. This is a genuine area of legal nuance in coal-producing regions and worth getting right rather than assuming.

faqs.q: How do you value a CBM well compared to a conventional oil well?
faqs.a: We look at the well's actual current production and decline behavior rather than applying a blanket formula across well types, since CBM wells follow a different production curve than conventional oil and gas wells.

items.name: Documents You Need to Sell
items.meta: Everything that typically goes in the closing folder for a mineral rights sale, from the original deed to the division order, and where to find each one.

sections.html:
Think of this as the folder a buyer will eventually ask you to build. Starting it early is the single easiest way to shorten your own closing.

Every mineral rights sale ends up needing roughly the same stack of paperwork, whether the interest is producing or not. Some of it you'll already have; some of it a title company will pull for you during their own research. Knowing the difference ahead of time keeps you from scrambling once an offer is on the table.

Not every document below applies to every seller. Treat this as a checklist to work through, not a requirement that every line be filled before you can start a conversation with a buyer.

sections.title: Proof of ownership
sections.html:
The most important document is whatever deed or instrument shows how you acquired the mineral interest, whether that's a deed from a previous purchase, a will or probate order if you inherited it, or a trust document if the interest is held in a trust. If you don't have the original, the county clerk or recorder's office where the minerals sit can usually provide a certified copy for a small fee.

For inherited interests where the deceased owner's name is still on record, you may also need an affidavit of heirship or a probate order showing how the interest passed to you, particularly if it changed hands more than once across generations without being formally re-deeded each time.

sections.title: Production and payment history
sections.html:
If the interest is producing, gather recent royalty check stubs or the operator's monthly statements, ideally the last twelve to twenty-four months if you have them. This is what a buyer uses to build the pricing multiple, and more history generally leads to a more confident offer rather than a conservative one hedged for uncertainty.

Also useful, though not always available to you directly: your most recent division order, which shows the decimal interest the operator has you recorded at, and any prior division orders if your interest changed size over time.

sections.title: Lease and legal paperwork
sections.html:
If your minerals are under an active lease, gather a copy of it, along with any amendments or ratifications signed since. This tells a buyer the royalty rate, the lease term, and whether it's held by production or approaching expiration, all of which affect value. If there's no current lease, note that as well, since unleased minerals get priced differently than leased ones.

Also worth pulling together: any correspondence from operators about pooling, unitization, or proposed drilling, since these often signal upcoming activity that a buyer will want to know about.

sections.title: Identification and closing logistics
sections.html: At closing you'll need government-issued identification for notarization, and if the interest is held by an entity, formation documents and proof of who's authorized to sign on the entity's behalf. Have your current mailing address and, if applicable, direct deposit information ready as well, since that's what gets updated on the new division order after closing.

sections.title: Documents specific to inherited or multi-owner interests
sections.html:
When minerals passed through a family across more than one generation without formal re-deeding at each step, gather whatever you can find connecting each transfer: death certificates, wills, and any probate court records. If a formal probate never happened, an affidavit of heirship prepared by an attorney can often bridge the gap, though the specific requirements vary by state.

If the interest is currently owned jointly by siblings or other relatives, having everyone's current contact information ready early helps, since most closings require every owner to sign, and tracking down a co-owner who's moved or lost touch with the rest of the family is one of the more common sources of delay.

faqs.q: What if you've lost your original deed?
faqs.a: That's common, especially with older or inherited interests. A certified copy can typically be obtained from the county clerk's office where the property is located for a modest fee.

faqs.q: Do you need your royalty statements if your minerals aren't leased or producing?
faqs.a: No. Unleased or non-producing minerals are priced on comparable sales and nearby activity instead, so payment history isn't part of that picture.

faqs.q: What is an affidavit of heirship and when do you need one?
faqs.a: It's a sworn statement establishing how a deceased owner's interest passed to heirs when there was no formal probate proceeding, or the deed was never updated. Title companies commonly require one for inherited interests without a clean paper trail.

faqs.q: Can you start the sale process before you've gathered every document?
faqs.a: Yes. Buyers can typically start title work with just a general sense of location and ownership and pull most of what's needed from county records as the process moves forward.

faqs.q: Who actually orders the title search, you or the buyer?
faqs.a: Almost always the buyer or their title company orders and pays for title work as part of due diligence, since it's their funds at risk if the title turns out to have a defect.

items.name: Mineral Deeds & Title Transfer
items.meta: How a mineral deed actually transfers title, from legal description to signature requirements to recording at the county clerk, explained step by step.

sections.html:
A mineral deed looks like a short document. What it takes to get one right, and get it recorded cleanly, is longer than the page count suggests.

The deed is the instrument that legally moves ownership of a mineral interest from you to a buyer. It sounds simple, but mineral deeds carry a few technical requirements that regular real estate deeds don't, and getting them wrong is one of the more common reasons a sale gets delayed after everyone has already agreed on price.

This page walks through what goes into the deed itself and what happens to it between signing and the moment it actually protects the buyer's ownership.

sections.title: The legal description has to be exact
sections.html:
Every mineral deed needs a legal description of the tract, beyond an address or a general location. In much of the country that means metes and bounds or a section-township-range description pulled from the original patent or a prior deed in the chain of title. If your deed is transferring a fractional interest rather than all the minerals under a tract, that fraction needs to be stated precisely, as a percentage or as net mineral acres, and it has to match what title research actually shows you own.

Mismatches here are one of the most common sources of delay. If the legal description in your old deed doesn't quite match current county plat records, that gets sorted out during title work, sometimes with a corrective deed or an affidavit of heirship if the discrepancy traces back to an inheritance.

Depth and formation limits sometimes appear in the description too. Older deeds occasionally reserved or excluded specific formations, or capped ownership at a certain depth, which matters more today than it did when the deed was written, since horizontal drilling now targets formations that weren't even part of the original conversation. A title examiner will flag this if it applies to your tract, and it may need to be addressed carefully in how the new deed is worded, so the buyer's rights match exactly what the seller actually intended to convey.

sections.title: Warranty type: what the deed actually promises
sections.html: Mineral deeds typically come in a few flavors. A general warranty deed has the seller guaranteeing clear title against all claims, past and present. A special warranty deed only document against claims arising during the seller's own ownership. A quitclaim or mineral deed without warranty simply conveys whatever interest the seller has, with no document at all. Buyers usually prefer a warranty deed of some kind; which type gets used is typically negotiated as part of the purchase agreement, not decided at the last minute.

sections.title: Signing requirements
sections.html: Mineral deeds generally need to be signed in front of a notary, and depending on the county, may need to meet specific formatting requirements for margins, font size, or the first page to be accepted for recording. If more than one person owns the interest, such as siblings who inherited minerals jointly, all owners typically need to sign, or a power of attorney needs to be on file for anyone who can't sign directly.

sections.title: Recording at the county clerk's office
sections.html:
Once signed, the deed gets recorded in the county where the minerals are located, which is what makes the transfer a matter of public record and establishes the buyer's priority against later claims. Recording usually happens through the title company or closing agent handling escrow, and a copy of the recorded deed, stamped with the county clerk's filing information, becomes part of your closing documents.

Recording can take anywhere from same-day to several weeks depending on the county's backlog, and until it's recorded, the transfer isn't fully protected against competing claims that might get filed in the meantime.

faqs.q: What's the difference between a mineral deed and a lease?
faqs.a: A deed permanently transfers ownership of the mineral interest itself. A lease grants an operator the right to explore and produce for a set term in exchange for royalty payments, while ownership stays with the mineral owner.

faqs.q: Do all co-owners have to sign the deed?
faqs.a: Generally yes, if the sale covers a jointly owned interest. Each owner typically needs to sign, or provide a valid power of attorney, before the deed can be recorded and the sale finalized.

faqs.q: What happens if the legal description doesn't match county records?
faqs.a: This gets caught during title work and usually resolved with a corrective deed, a survey, or an affidavit clarifying the chain of title, though it can add time to closing.

faqs.q: How long does it take for a deed to be recorded?
faqs.a: It varies by county, from same-day in smaller, well-staffed clerk's offices to several weeks in busier counties, especially during periods of heavy drilling activity when filing volume spikes.

faqs.q: Do you need an attorney to review the deed before signing?
faqs.a: It's not always required, but having an attorney review the deed and warranty type is a reasonable step, particularly for larger interests or ones with a complicated ownership history.

items.name: Division Orders Explained
items.meta: What a division order is, why operators require one after a mineral rights sale, and how transfer orders redirect royalty payments to the new owner.

sections.html:
The deed makes the sale legal. The division order is what actually makes the operator start paying the right person.

A division order is one of the least understood documents in a mineral rights transaction, mostly because it shows up at the very end, after the price is agreed and the deed is signed, when everyone's attention has already moved on. It's also one of the documents that most directly affects when royalty checks actually start arriving in the new owner's name.

This page explains what a division order is, why it exists separately from the deed, and what to expect in the weeks after closing.

sections.title: What a division order actually is
sections.html:
A division order is a statement, issued by the operator, showing the decimal interest they've calculated for each owner in a well or unit, and how they intend to pay royalties based on that decimal. It's the operator's own accounting document, not a title document, which is why the deed and the division order are handled separately even though they're connected.

The decimal interest reflects your ownership fraction combined with the royalty rate in the governing lease, translated into a single number the operator's payment system uses. A common decimal might look like 0.00234375, representing a small fractional share of total production from a spacing unit that may include hundreds of net mineral acres and multiple owners.

sections.title: Why buyers need a new one after closing
sections.html:
When you sell your interest, the operator is still paying royalties under your old division order until they're formally notified of the sale and issue a new one in the buyer's name. This is why closing on a producing interest doesn't instantly redirect payments. The buyer typically sends the operator a copy of the recorded deed along with a transfer order or a request to update the division order.

Operators process these on their own schedule, and it's genuinely normal for this step to take one to three royalty payment cycles, sometimes longer if the operator's division order department has a backlog or if the sale involves a fractional interest that requires recalculating decimals for multiple owners in the unit.

sections.title: What sellers should watch for
sections.html:
If you sell a producing interest, you may receive one or two more royalty checks after closing before the operator's paperwork catches up. Depending on how your purchase agreement was written, those checks may need to be forwarded to the buyer or accounted for in a post-closing settlement, so it's worth confirming which approach applies before you deposit anything.

It's also worth double-checking that the decimal interest on any new division order you're asked to sign matches what you actually own or sold. Errors happen, especially in units with many small owners, and signing a division order with an incorrect decimal can be harder to unwind after the fact than catching it beforehand.

sections.title: How this ties back to the closing paperwork
sections.html:
The purchase agreement itself often addresses division order timing directly, spelling out who's entitled to production revenue for the period straddling the closing date and how any checks that arrive under the seller's name after closing should be handled. Reading that section carefully before signing avoids a confusing conversation later about a check that shows up weeks after the deed was already recorded.

For buyers, tracking down every operator involved when a seller holds interests spread across multiple units or wells can take longer than the closing itself, since each operator has its own division order department working on its own timeline, independent of how quickly the deed was recorded at the courthouse. Patience here is normal, not a sign that something has gone wrong with the sale.

faqs.q: Is a division order the same as a deed?
faqs.a: No. The deed is the legal instrument that transfers ownership. The division order is the operator's internal accounting document that determines how royalty checks get calculated and mailed.

faqs.q: How long after closing until royalty checks go to the new owner?
faqs.a: It commonly takes one to three payment cycles for an operator to process the transfer and issue a new division order, though this varies by operator and can take longer if paperwork is incomplete.

faqs.q: What if you get a royalty check after you've already sold your interest?
faqs.a: This happens when the operator hasn't yet processed the transfer. Whether that check gets forwarded to the buyer or handled through a post-closing adjustment depends on how your purchase agreement addressed it.

faqs.q: Do you have to sign a new division order to sell your interest?
faqs.a: Signing a division order isn't what transfers ownership, the deed does that, but the buyer will typically need to sign or acknowledge a new one for the operator to begin paying them directly.

faqs.q: Can a division order decimal be wrong?
faqs.a: Yes, particularly in units with many owners or complicated fractional interests. It's worth reviewing the decimal against your known ownership share before signing anything the operator sends.

items.name: Reading Your Royalty Statements
items.meta: How to read a royalty statement line by line, including decimal interest, deductions, and proration periods, and why those details shape a purchase offer.

sections.html:
A royalty statement is dense on purpose. Once you can read it line by line, it stops being confusing and starts being the most useful document you own.

If your minerals are producing, the statement that arrives with your royalty check is also the document most likely to determine your purchase offer. Buyers read these closely, and it helps to understand what they're looking at before you hand a stack of them over.

Statements vary in format by operator, but most cover the same core information laid out in roughly the same order.

sections.title: The proration period
sections.html:
Every statement covers a proration period, typically a calendar month, showing production and sales that occurred during that window. Because oil and gas accounting runs behind actual production, a statement dated for a given month often reflects production from one or two months earlier. This lag is normal and not a sign anything is wrong; it just means the check you get in March is usually paying for January's production, not March's.

When comparing multiple months to spot a trend, always compare by proration period, not by the date the check arrived, or the trend will look distorted by timing rather than actual production changes.

sections.title: Decimal interest and gross value
sections.html: Your decimal interest, the same number that appears on your division order, is applied to the well or unit's total production and sales value to calculate your gross share. This is usually shown as a small decimal, since most owners hold a fraction of a percent in any given unit. The statement should show the gross value before deductions, which is your starting point for understanding what you're actually being paid on.

sections.title: Deductions and net payment
sections.html:
Most statements subtract post-production costs, things like gathering, transportation, processing, and marketing, before arriving at your net payment. Whether these deductions are allowed depends on the specific language in the governing lease; some older leases prohibit certain deductions entirely, while many modern leases permit them. Comparing gross value to net payment tells you what percentage is being deducted, which is worth tracking over time since it can change as gathering and processing arrangements change.

Severance and ad valorem taxes are also typically deducted at the state and county level before you receive payment, separate from post-production costs, and are usually broken out as their own line.

sections.title: Why buyers ask for a stack of these
sections.html: One statement shows a snapshot. Twelve to twenty-four consecutive months show a trend, and trend is what a buyer actually prices, since it reveals where a well sits on its decline curve and how volatile the payments have been month to month. A steadily declining but predictable trend supports a more confident offer than a single strong month with no history behind it.

sections.title: Other lines worth checking
sections.html:
Most statements also show the well or unit name, the API number identifying the specific well, and sometimes the price per barrel or per thousand cubic feet used to calculate that month's value. Comparing that price against publicly available benchmark prices for the same period can flag whether an operator's realized price looks unusually low, which occasionally happens due to gathering or marketing arrangements worth asking about.

If your statement covers more than one well within the same unit, look for a breakdown by well rather than a single combined figure, since it's harder to judge decline behavior accurately when production from a newer well is blended together with an older one on the same page. Ask the operator for a well-level breakdown directly if your statement doesn't already provide one, since most will supply it on request even when the default format doesn't.

faqs.q: Why does your royalty check amount change every month?
faqs.a: Commodity prices, production volume, and deductions all shift month to month, so it's normal for payments to fluctuate rather than stay flat, particularly in the early years of a well's life.

faqs.q: What's the difference between gross value and net payment on your statement?
faqs.a: Gross value is your decimal interest applied to total production value before deductions. Net payment is what's left after post-production costs and taxes are subtracted, which is the amount you actually receive.

faqs.q: Why is your statement dated for a month that already passed by a lot?
faqs.a: Oil and gas accounting typically runs one to two months behind actual production, so the proration period on your statement usually reflects earlier production than the date the check arrived.

faqs.q: Can you dispute deductions you don't think are allowed under your lease?
faqs.a: Yes, if you believe deductions conflict with your lease terms, that's worth raising with the operator directly or with an attorney, since lease language on post-production costs varies and controls what's permitted.

faqs.q: How many months of statements should you keep?
faqs.a: Keeping at least the last twelve to twenty-four months is useful both for your own records and because that's typically the window a buyer will want to review when building a purchase offer.

items.name: How to Sell Mineral Rights
items.meta: A step-by-step anatomy of a mineral rights purchase, from first inquiry to recorded deed, so you know what each stage actually involves before you sign anything.

sections.html:
Selling mineral rights is not one event. It is a sequence of smaller decisions, each with its own paperwork, and knowing the sequence is what keeps a seller from getting rushed.

Most people who search for how to sell mineral rights are really asking a narrower question: what happens after accepting an offer? This page walks through the anatomy of a purchase in the order it actually unfolds, so you can see where the leverage sits, where the paperwork slows down, and where a seller who understands the process tends to end up better off than one who does not.

None of this replaces your own attorney or CPA. It is meant to make the conversation with them shorter, because you will already know the vocabulary.

sections.title: Stage one: figuring out what you actually own
sections.html:
Before any number gets discussed, a buyer needs to know what interest you hold. Mineral rights and royalty interests are not the same thing, and neither is the same as a working interest with cost obligations attached. Some owners hold minerals under land they never lived on, inherited from a grandparent's allotment or a family farm sold decades ago with the minerals reserved. Others hold a royalty interest carved out of a lease, which pays a share of production but carries no drilling costs.

This stage usually starts with you gathering whatever paperwork you have: a deed, a division order, an old lease, a royalty check stub. A serious buyer will ask for a legal description, beyond a county and a rough acreage, because pricing and title work both depend on the specific tract.

sections.title: Stage two: the offer and what it is actually based on
sections.html:
A written offer typically references recent royalty payment history if the interest is producing, or nearby leasing and permitting activity if it is undeveloped. Offers on producing interests are commonly framed as a multiple of recent monthly or quarterly royalty checks, adjusted for how fast that production is expected to decline. Offers on non-producing acreage lean more on comparable transactions in the area and how close active rigs or permits are to your tract.

Treat the first number as a starting point, not a final one. Ask what data it is built on, and ask whether the buyer has run title yet. An offer made before title work is preliminary by nature, and it should be treated that way by both sides.

sections.title: Stage three: signing, but not closing
sections.html:
When you agree to terms, you sign a purchase and sale agreement, not a deed. The PSA sets the price, the closing timeline, and the conditions the buyer can still walk away under, most commonly a title defect that materially changes value. Read the due diligence period carefully. It is normal for a buyer to have thirty to sixty days to examine title before funding.

This is also the stage where earnest money sometimes changes hands, held by a title company or escrow agent rather than paid directly to either party, so that neither side can walk off with funds mid-transaction.

sections.title: Stage four: title work, escrow, and the deed
sections.html:
The buyer's title work will check the courthouse records for liens, unreleased old leases, competing claims from other heirs, and whether the legal description in your paperwork actually matches the county's plat records. Gaps here are common with older or inherited interests and are usually fixable, but they take time.

Once title clears, closing happens through escrow: funds and the signed mineral deed are both held by a neutral party and released simultaneously, so payment and transfer happen at the same moment rather than one side trusting the other to follow through second.

sections.title: Stage five: after the deed is recorded
sections.html: Recording the deed at the county clerk's office is what makes the sale a matter of public record and protects the buyer's interest against later claims. If the property is producing, the buyer still has to notify the operator and get a new division order issued before royalty checks redirect to them, which can take one to three payment cycles depending on the operator's paperwork backlog.

faqs.q: How long does the whole process take from offer to closing?
faqs.a: It varies with how clean the title is and how quickly the county clerk's office processes documents, but a straightforward transaction with clear title commonly closes in three to six weeks. Complicated heirship or an unreleased old lease can add well beyond that.

faqs.q: Do you need a lawyer to sell mineral rights?
faqs.a: It is not always required, but for anything beyond a small fractional interest it is worth having an attorney review the purchase agreement and deed before you sign, especially if the interest passed through inheritance.

faqs.q: Can you sell only part of your mineral rights?
faqs.a: Yes. Owners frequently sell a percentage of their interest, or the rights under one tract while keeping others, and a deed can be drafted to convey exactly that fraction.

faqs.q: What if you can't find your original deed or lease paperwork?
faqs.a: That is common with inherited interests. A buyer can typically pull the relevant county records themselves during title work, though having whatever documents you do have speeds things up.

faqs.q: Will selling affect royalty checks you're already receiving?
faqs.a: Checks continue under your name until the new division order is processed after closing. After that, payments redirect to the buyer for production going forward.

items.name: What Are Mineral Rights Worth?
items.meta: Learn how mineral rights purchase prices actually get built from royalty history, decline curves, and comparable sales, instead of chasing a single per-acre number.

sections.html:
There is no lookup table for what mineral rights are worth. There is a method, and once you understand the method the number stops feeling arbitrary.

Almost every owner who calls a buyer starts with the same question: what are these mineral rights worth? The honest answer is that it depends on which of two very different pricing methods applies to your interest, and neither one produces a fixed number that holds still for long.

This page walks through both methods so that when you get an offer, you can tell whether it was built on real inputs or guessed at.

sections.title: Producing minerals: the multiple-of-checks approach
sections.html:
If your interest is already generating royalty income, buyers typically price it as a multiple of your recent monthly or quarterly payments, annualized and then adjusted downward for expected decline. Unconventional wells, the kind common in shale plays, tend to produce steeply in the first one to three years and then flatten into a long, low tail. A buyer pricing that stream has to guess how far along the decline curve your well already sits, because a check today from a five-year-old well is worth a very different multiple than the same size check from a well six months old.

This is why two owners with identical current royalty checks can get different offers. The one on the older well is closer to the flat part of the curve, meaning less future decline risk, and that typically supports a higher multiple. The one on the newer well still has a steep drop-off ahead, which a buyer has to discount for.

sections.title: Non-producing minerals: comparable sales and proximity
sections.html:
Undeveloped mineral acreage with no lease or no well yet is priced differently, because there is no check to build a multiple from. Buyers instead look at recent per-acre sales of comparable tracts nearby, active permitting within a mile or two, and whether your acreage sits inside a unit that operators have shown interest in leasing. Acreage in the core of an active play with recent permits close by will typically be quoted at a different range than acreage on the flank of the same play with no nearby activity, and that range moves with permitting and rig counts, not on a fixed schedule.

Be wary of any number quoted with total confidence and no context about nearby activity. A serious buyer will explain what comparable data the number is drawn from, and will usually hedge it as a range rather than a single figure, because that is genuinely how the market works.

sections.title: What actually moves the number
sections.html:
Beyond the two methods above, a handful of factors push value up or down inside whatever range applies to your interest: net mineral acres versus gross acres in the unit, whether you own all the minerals under the tract or a fractional share, the specific formation and its historical productivity in that county, and how many operators are actively drilling nearby versus just holding leases without activity.

Risking also matters more than most owners expect. A buyer has to weigh what a well might produce, and separately, the chance it underperforms, gets shut in, or the operator delays development entirely. That risk gets baked into the multiple or the per-acre range, which is part of why offers on paper interests never quite match what a producing neighbor's acre sold for.

Title itself factors into the number too. A tract with a clean, easily verified chain of ownership tends to close faster and with fewer surprises than one with unresolved heirship or a decades-old lease that was never formally released, and buyers sometimes build a little cushion into an early offer to account for that uncertainty before title work confirms exactly what's involved.

faqs.q: Is there a standard per-acre price for mineral rights?
faqs.a: No. Per-acre pricing depends heavily on play, county, proximity to active permits, and current market conditions, and it shifts as those change, so any flat number quoted without that context should be treated skeptically.

faqs.q: Why did your neighbor get a different offer than you for similar acreage?
faqs.a: Even adjacent tracts can differ in net mineral acres owned, formation rights included, lease status, and whether recent permits sit closer to one tract than the other, all of which shift the range a buyer will quote.

faqs.q: Do royalty checks alone determine value?
faqs.a: They're the starting point for producing interests, but the multiple applied depends on how far along the well's decline curve you are, beyond the size of the current check alone.

faqs.q: Will oil and gas prices affect your offer?
faqs.a: Commodity prices influence both current royalty income and how aggressively operators are permitting new wells nearby, so yes, offers do move with broader market activity.

faqs.q: Should you get multiple offers before selling?
